subtopic: MR. HOWARD  RESPONSIBILITY OF JUSTICE MINISTER UNDER BILL OF RIGHTS
MR. HOWARD  RESPONSIBILITY OF JUSTICE MINISTER UNDER BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting this house and every member of it. My question of privilege involves the failure or neglect on the part of the Minister of Justice to discharge a responsibility and a duty which parliament gave to him. That responsibility and duty is that which is contained within section 3 of the bill of rights and the regulations made with respect to section 3.
I wonder whether I should read to you the relevant part of section 3 of the Canadian Bill of Rights, which is as follows:
The Minister of Justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the privy council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons, in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part and he shall report any such inconsistency to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity.
The regulations pursuant to that section provide the mechanics for dealing with bills presented to or introduced in the House of Commons, and regulation P.C. 1960/1792 sets up the procedure and allows in clause 3(b) of the regulation that the minister shall:
-cause to be affixed to each of the copies thereof- -that is, copies of bills-
-so received from the Clerk of the House of Commons a certificate, in a form approved by the minister and signed by the deputy minister of justice, stating that the bill has been examined as required by the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Mr. Speaker, the total number of bills introduced in the House of Commons this session prior to yesterday was 109. Of those bills, the period of time which elapsed between their transmission by the Clerk of the House of Commons to the Minister of Justice and their return to the Clerk with the affixed and approved stamp on the front of them, indicating that they had been examined pursuant to the bill of rights, was
statistically as follows. There were six of those bills in which the time which elapsed was only one day. There were 40 of those bills in which the period of time which elapsed was two days. There were 19 of them in which the period of time which had elapsed was three days. There were 16 bills in which the period of time which had elapsed was four days. Ten of them took five days. Five of them took six days. Three consumed a period of eight days. One of them took 13 days. Another one took 14 days; and six of them had no indication of the number of days on the approved stamp affixed to the front of the bill, although there was an indication that they had been received back by the House of Commons in a period of time not longer than eight days.
Even with respect to the one which took 13 days and the one which took 14 days to-examine, that was over the Christmas and New Year's holiday. Hence we can extract from that figure a reasonable number of days upon which the people were not working and thus were not examining bills.
There is one bill which was introduced on October 1 of last year, at the start of this session, and which has not been so returned and, I submit, has not been examined as required by section 3 of the bill of rights. That date is 123 or 124 days ago. That bill is C-14, an act respecting Indians, one which I myself submitted.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this question of privilege is that the Minister of Justice, either by failure or neglect, has not examined that particular bill and has not,, as is required by the bill of rights, returned it to the House of Commons. Accordingly, based upon that premise, it is a prima facie case of privilege and I move as follows, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the standing committee on privileges and elections be authorized and instructed to inquire into and study the responsibilities attendant upon the Minister of Justice by virtue of section 3 of the Canadian Bill of Rights and whether those responsibilities were properly carried out with respect to Bill C-14, an act respecting Indians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlineau (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH COBALT REFINERY FOR SILVER BULLION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that the governor in council has approved the treasury board recommendation to authorize the director of the Royal Canadian Mint to reach an agreement with the Cobalt Refinery Limited of Toronto, Ontario, for the supplying of silver bullion.
The agreement would become effective on April 1, 1963, and would be for a period of five years. It stipulates that Cobalt Refinery will deliver to the mint from 2 to 6 million ounces of silver per year, at competitive prices to be determined by negotiation every year the agreement is in force.
Cobalt Refinery Limited operates a silver refinery at Cobalt, Ontario. Its contract with the Canadian mint will enable it to buy larger quantities of silver ore concentrates already produced in the Cobalt and Gowganda districts. Since the closing of the Deloro Silver Refinery in 1961, those concentrates have been shipped to other countries to be refined.
It is expected that the transaction will help maintain in operation a new silver ore processing plant in Canada and that it will also benefit the mining operations in that region of Ontario.

It is to be hoped that on the strength of what is now available under this agreement Canadian producers will be able to send all their silver to this refinery for treatment.

Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned Wednesday evening last I was recommending greater participation by the industrial development bank to the setting up and creation of new industries in Canada.
Certainly, if we want to reduce unemployment and recapture economic control over our industries, which are now in Amer-
(Mr. Herridge.l
ican hands, we must also find the financial means required by our industrial development.
I should like also to draw the attention of the house to a comment found in this morning's press, to the effect that the lack of development of the Canadian financial system, the lack of expansion of the monetary supply is at the very root of unemployment now prevailing in Canada and of the "nondevelopment" of our industries.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the house and this government are duty bound to ponder seriously that lack of financial possibilities for the development of our industry in Canada.
I think that the present regulations of the industrial development bank will have to be modified in order to supply the capital required for the multiplication of Canadian industries.
Of course, it is perhaps difficult for the government to require private enterprise to create new industries. But I believe that the Department of Trade and Commerce, which must provide for the development of our industries, is in a position to convince our industrialists that certain imported goods could be manufactured economically in Canada. It is the duty of that department to make the necessary publicity to that effect, and it is also its duty to develop the interest of our industrialists toward certain particular fields.
In my opinion, it is up to the government to provide the necessary facilities for those industries to establish themselves preferably in communities where unemployment is most acute.
The government's winter works program has greatly contributed to the stabilization of the economy. However, I should like to point out to the minister that as long as the unemployment situation has not improved substantially in Canada, he will have to allow certain works to be carried out at a more appropriate time of the year.
At present, the program is in effect from October to May but I call the minister's attention to the fact that certain projects can be undertaken by municipalities only in the fall, a period which is too short in some cases.
It should be taken into account how ridiculous it is that workers are idle in the summer and can only find jobs for a few months during

the coldest period of the year, that is in January and February.
This is not logical because those workers who were unable to find jobs in the fine summer months, must buy warmer and very expensive clothes to work outside in the winter months. Now, they often work only a few days and their earnings are barely enough to pay for those clothes.
There is also another aspect to winter works. I should like to point out in particular the serious problem which will probably prompt several municipalities to curtail their winter works. A great number of our municipalities are hard put to find the necessary funds to take part in the winter works program, because we know that even though the government pays 50 per cent of the labour costs, nevertheless municipalities must provide 10 per cent and pay, in addition, the material, equipment and machinery required for the carrying out of those winter works.
In fact, most of our municipalities are so involved in debt that they cannot spend any more money without increasing the already too heavy burden of taxes resting upon the citizens' shoulders.
I believe the only possible solution would be that the government set up a municipal development bank to enable our municipalities to borrow on easy terms, to increase their contribution to the winter works program, and even to carry out certain projects which nearly all of them have been looking forward to for a long time.
Mr. Chairman, the government has also shown that it was conscious of the problem arising from automation and its effects by introducing Bill No. C-83 at the beginning of the session. When this bill comes before us again, we shall give it a more thorough consideration. Since my time is running out, I shall await another opportunity to discuss it at greater length.
The Minister of Labour now has in his hands several briefs which were submitted to him by trade unions, as well as the Gill report on the unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service. Worthy recommendations have been put forward by everybody and I hope that with the co-operation of all the groups concerned with the matter-there is quite a number of them-improvements can be made to increase the efficiency of this branch which is trying to find jobs for the unemployed.

I will leave the more thorough discussion of the problems concerning unemployment insurance to others who wish to take part in this debate.
Before bringing my remarks to a close, I should like to point out to the minister my satisfaction in seeing that he is fully conscious of the problems resulting from unemployment in our country, but I believe other measures as well would also be desirable besides those which have been adopted so far. I am myself interested in labour conditions, and I know that the solutions are not easy to find. However, with the co-operation of the members of the cabinet and of his colleagues, I believe the minister should obtain, even demand that a greater share of the estimates be provided for areas which are more heavily affected by unemployment. On the other hand, I know that their budgets are limited but, nevertheless, since the Minister of Public Works is responsible for the carrying out of government projects in the country, he should take into consideration, while preparing his budget, the areas affected and provide special projects for them. The areas with surplus manpower should benefit from a greater share of the budget. In these areas, several projects have been submitted to the minister concerned. Therefore, I should like above all to ask the Minister of Labour to exert pressure on his colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton) to put at the disposal of those areas larger amounts of money for the works likely to improve their economy.
The formula is merely a temporary one. Only an increase in the number of industries will bring stability and will substantially reduce unemployment in the various sections of the country.
Statistics reveal that we have 414,000 unemployed in the country, 154,000 of whom are in the province of Quebec. In my opinion, this situation should make the cabinet members conscious of their responsibility to adopt means likely to reduce unemployment in all parts of this country. In fact, the province of Quebec is just as much entitled as any other part of the country, if not more so, to its share of government expenditures and investments.

I think it is entirely fitting that, having discussed yesterday the No. 1 problem which Canada faces in the field of foreign affairs, we should devote today to discussing the No. 1 problem which Canada faces in the field of domestic affairs, namely that of unemployment. It seems to me that when the estimates of the Minister of Labour come before the committee the minister ought to deal primarily with this problem of unemployment, and that the committee ought likewise to devote its time primarily to this problem.
Many of us recall that when the session opened the government, when it brought down the speech from the throne, promised to create a million new jobs. Since that time the government has created many new jobs. However, the trouble is that all these new jobs have gone to defeated Tory candidates. In the meantime, according to the latest unemployment figures which we have, covering the month of December, 1962, 414,000 Canadians were unemployed. This figure represented 6.3 per cent of the labour force. That figure meant that 414,000 men and women did not have jobs. It meant that they and their families were suffering. It meant that they were deprived of the opportunity of taking an equal part in the development of this country.
I think it is essential that the minister and this committee should realize the magnitude of that figure; I refer to the figure of 414,000 wage earners and salary earners who are out of work. That figure is equivalent to the entire male labour force of the province of British Columbia. The situation is just the same as it would be if every man in British Columbia were without a job. Surely under those circumstances the committee would be able to persuade the Minister of Labour and the government that the unemployment situation was critical, that we faced an emergency condition, and that something ought to be done about it.
I am going to discuss later what the government has done about it and what we think it ought to do about it. Before doing that, however, let me point out to the committee that the figure of 414,000 unemployed is equal to two thirds of the labour force of the Atlantic region. This unemployment figure is one which although it is less than that of a year ago, remains nevertheless a figure which ought to be of grave concern

to the minister, the government, the committee and the house. If the entire male labour force of British Columbia were out of work, or if two thirds of the entire labour force of the Atlantic region were out of work, this committee would demand that the government mobilize the resources of this country in order to put those people back to work. I suggest that under the present circumstances we ought to treat the situation as being just as critical. I suggest that we ought to require the minister and the government to mobilize the resources of the country in order to make sure that those 414,000 people go back to work at the earliest possible opportunity.
It is easy in Canada to get people worked up over a strike. Editorial writers rush into print as soon as a strike or a lockout takes place. However, the time lost as a result of strikes over the last 50 years of Canada's history averages less than 0.2 per cent of the total working time each year. The secretary of labour in the United States Mr. Wirtz, said recently that he was appalled by the realization that in the United States more man hours were lost as a result of unemployment in 1962 than were lost from strikes in the preceding 35 years. Yet editorial writers become concerned about the loss of employment, the loss of man hours and the loss of production which results from strikes and lockouts while this tremendous problem of unemployment which we have had in Canada for many years has ceased to agitate them.
I put the matter in this vivid way in order to bring home to the members of the committee the importance of the problem. If the entire male labour force of British Columbia were out of work we believe that editorial writers would not accept half measures; they would demand action on the part of the government. Instead, when facing just as critical a problem as that, what do we have from the government? No one suggests that the Minister of Labour has not tackled this problem in all sincerity. What we object to is the fact that the government's program has not been adequate to meet the emergency. What we object to is the fact that the government's program affects only the fringes of the unemployment problem.
What have the government done about unemployment? They have instituted a do it now program. They have instituted a winter works program. They have instituted a system of capital grants to the provinces to enable the provinces to carry on technical and vocational training. All these things reflect credit upon the minister and the government, but they do not go far enough. They do not get to the root of the problem. They

constitute a form of unemployment after-care. Nothing has been done to eradicate the hard core unemployment problem, a problem that we have had in this country for many years. This hard core of unemployment has existed ever since world war II.
I know that earlier this week the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate told the house that during the 12 years following the war we had full employment in this country. Those are the very words he used; they appear in Hansard. I think it will be acknowledged in all parts of the house, even among members of his own party, that the hon. member's statement was entirely inaccurate. As a matter of fact his own leader, the Leader of the Opposition, during the debate on the speech from the throne told us that during the 12 years following the war under a Liberal regime unemployment averaged 3 per cent each year. I do not blame the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for not listening to the speeches of his leader, but I suggest that at least he ought to read them occasionally if only to avoid being unaware of the abrupt changes in policy that the Leader of the Opposition makes from time to time.
Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, I apologize to the hon. gentleman because I was not listening to his speech at all. Could he tell me what he was complaining about in my conduct?

I was not complaining. I do not think the hon. member's conduct can be a matter of complaint. I was talking about a speech the hon. member made in the house earlier this week in which he said, and this appears in Hansard, that during the 12 years following the second world war we had full employment in this country. I pointed out that this was entirely at variance with what the Leader of the Opposition said during the debate on the speech from the throne, when the Leader of the Opposition stated that during those 12 years unemployment averaged 3 per cent each year. I suggested to the hon. member that he should read the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition even if he was not prepared to listen to them.
At any rate, the point I was seeking to make was that the statement that we had full employment in this country for 12 years following the war is nothing more or less than arrogant nonsense. Many of us had friends and relatives who were unemployed for years during that 12 year period, and I suggest it is not doing justice to the problem or being fair to the house to make statements of that kind.
Today unemployment is declining. From 1953 to 1961 unemployment rose from 3 per cent to 7.2 per cent on the basis of the 27507-3-211J

annual average. During the same period the average during the winter months rose from 4.3 per cent in 1953 to 11 per cent in 1961.
Could the hon. gentleman say what figures those are? Are they bureau of statistics figures?

Yes, they are. In 1962 the unemployment figure was 5.9 per cent. This represents a decline but, as I said earlier, this represented 414,000 unemployed. The Minister of Labour and the government do not know why unemployment rose sharply from 1953 to 1961. They do not know why it declined slightly from 1961 to 1962. They do not know whether it is going to rise again. They do not know whether it is going to decline further. They do not know what to do about the hard core unemployment that we have had in this country for so many years. The government simply do not know where unemployment comes from, and I suggest they do not know where it goes.
What is most regrettable about the vast unemployment that we have in this country is not the loss of production involved but the demoralizing effect that idleness has upon men and women. Enforced idleness breeds a sense of frustration and uselessness, a consciousness of personal degradation, and this is far more damaging to our society than the loss of production which their idleness represents.
The government's program is one which over a six year period has proved inadequate by any standard. The government have had almost six years to cope with unemployment and do something about it, and they have failed utterly. After six years in office unemployment averaged almost 6 per cent last year. We had 414,000 Canadians unemployed in December, 1962, after the government had had six years to do something about the problem. Many of us recall the empty promise that the Prime Minister made during the election campaign of 1958, when he said that no one would suffer from unemployment as long as he was Prime Minister.
In view of the government's failure, why does the government not adopt a program of genuine economic planning? This is the means by which other countries in the world have cured the unemployment problem. This is how the countries of western Europe and the Scandinavian countries have achieved prosperity and full employment. Why does the government persist in refusing to adopt a program of genuine economic planning? This would involve the expansion of public investment and the regulation of private investment. It would involve the location and relocation of industry. It would involve other

Supply-Labour
measures which come under the heading ot modern, genuine, economic planning.
Why does the government not adopt such a program? After all, what is more important than the provision of jobs for more than 400,000 Canadians who together with their families are suffering, who are not able to enjoy the good things of life that should be the right of every citizen in a country with the abundance that Canada has? What is more important, to provide these people with jobs or to continue to pay homage, as the government does, to economic cliches that have no validity under present day conditions?
When we in the New Democratic party talk about full employment we are talking about something that cannot really be measured statistically. We believe that we will never have full employment in this country until there are more jobs than there are people to fill them. When we reach that situation, Mr. Chairman, it will mean that if there are people moving from job to job, if there are people temporarily unemployed, all of them will live secure in the knowledge that there is useful work for them to do when they are able to do it and when they are required to undertake it.
Speakers in the government party and in the Liberal party, as well as spokesmen for some segments of business and industry in this country, have talked about what they call tolerable levels of unemployment. We in this party do not talk about tolerable levels of unemployment; we regard unemployment as intolerable.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is not just the manual workers, the craftsmen and the labourers who are the victims of unemployment in Canada today. The white collar worker is increasingly becoming the victim of unemployment. We are all aware of the enormous effect which automation has had upon those engaged in manual work. But we should all realize, and this was apparent from a study made by the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour a year ago, that although automation has increased the number of people required to tabulate and administer and distribute the products of our industrial machine, office mechanization and automation has already cut into that increase. The rate of increase of employment for the white collar worker is already declining. Office mechanization and automation has resulted in the displacement of people employed in sales, administrative and clerical work.
As a matter of fact, an article appeared in the Globe and Mail for November 23, 1962

headed "Automation May Soon Cut Middle-Management Ranks". It is a report by Ronald Anderson and reads in part as follows:
Automation, which has been blamed for high unemployment among unskilled workers, may soon cut into the ranks of middle-management.
Professor J. A. Sarjeant of the University of Toronto school of business told a graduate seminar this week the number of middle-management jobs will be reduced during the next ten years as computors take over many of the planning operations.
Now, Mr. Chairman, business plans ahead, industry plans ahead, so why should not the government of Canada plan ahead? It is essential that the government plan ahead, that the government set some course for Canada's economy, that the government lay down an economic blueprint for this country; otherwise the unemployment problem will get worse and worse as the years go by. It is going to have an increasing effect not only upon the manual worker but also upon the white collar worker.
We in this party believe that in years past we have been governed in this country by people who felt no sense of challenge; we have been governed by people who had neither the imagination nor the will to grapple with the difficulties we face. We have a Prime Minister who cannot make up his mind. We have a Leader of the Opposition who keeps changing his mind.
We observed them yesterday indulging in childish recriminations. These people have no solutions, they offer no solutions to the enormous problems that face us. They denounce a party that proposes a program of genuine economic planning and refer to that program as "magic nostrums". At the same time they propose, for purely political considerations, policies of debt free money. The two party system in this country is today a thing of the past because the two old parties have utterly failed to comprehend the problems that Canada faces in the second half of the twentieth century. We saw yesterday their paucity of ideas and the inconsistency of their policies in relation to foreign affairs. We have seen in this debate, as we have in previous debates during this parliament, evidence of the fact they are at a loss to know what to do about unemployment.
We in this party, Mr. Chairman, believe it is the responsibility of the government of this country to plan our economy to make sure that we achieve prosperity and full employment, to make sure there is useful work for every man and woman who wants to work. We believe it is the responsibility of the government of this country to bring about that situation. We think it could be done if only the government had the imagination and

the will to do it, because it has been done in so many other countries in other parts of the world.
We in the New Democratic party, Mr. Chairman, so long as this parliament lasts will fight to make sure that the government discharges its responsibilities to the people of Canada, and more particularly to ensure that this government discharges its responsibilities to the unemployed of Canada by providing jobs for people who should have had them long ago.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Labour upon the tremendous work he is doing in his department. I must say that the minister is not only familiar with labour problems and with employment, but he is also an authority on agriculture. I have had the privilege of having the minister speak in my constituency, and to say the least I was very much surprised that a person in his occupation would be so familiar with agriculture in the west. My people were really much impressed with his knowledge of this subject.
With this background of knowledge about agriculture and agricultural problems, I should like to bring to his attention one problem with which we are faced in the west. I refer to the problem of farm labour. Over the years science and technology have advanced to the point where some of our farms are getting bigger and some of our farms are shrinking in size. As a result the farm labourer seeks employment somewhere else. One reason a farm labourer seeks employment somewhere else is the discrimination against farm labour. His counterpart may seek employment in the cities and have available to him the advantages of unemployment insurance. This is not available to the farm labourer. I was very much disturbed in 1957 when I read that another class of employee had been covered by unemployment insurance. I refer to the fishermen. In 1957 it was not only the employees in the fishing industry who were covered by unemployment insurance but also the self employed fishermen.
Before I continue I should like to make one statement, and it is this. I am not against fishermen receiving the benefits of unemployment insurance; far from it. If there is a problem in the fishing industry it should have been taken care of under the Unemployment Insurance Act or by other means. At the time the then minister of fisheries, Mr. Sinclair, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate saw to it that the act was amended to give benefits to unemployed fishermen, there was not one mem-
Supply-Labour
ber of the Liberal party or of the Liberal ministry who was concerned about the unemployed farm labourer. This was the time when they should have made representations, when the farm labourers should also have been covered by insurance, but this was not done.
I have brought this problem of the unemployed farm labourer to the attention of the house on many occasions.
And I supported you many times.

However, since a royal commission was appointed in 1961 I could not continue introducing bills and bringing this matter to the attention of parliament until the report of that commission was tabled. That commission has done good work in reaching some conclusions and recommendations, but there is one point on which I cannot agree with the report. Paragraph 20 of the report contains this statement:
We recommend that the general principle be followed of extending coverage as broadly as possible so long as the necessary administrative procedures may be carried out to see to it that the rules of the plan are adhered to in a satisfactory fashion.
That is dealing with farm labourers, but on the other hand the commission says it is not able to recommend administrative procedures. What is the difference between administrative procedures for the farm labourer and administrative procedures for the self employed fisherman? If it was possible to include the self employed fishermen without encountering administrative difficulties, then I am certain farm labourers should also have been included. In my opinion this was discrimination against the farm labourers.
I would like the minister to give this particular paragraph of the report his earnest consideration when he comes to deal with the matter. From personal experience I know many small farmers experience difficulties in obtaining labour during the harvest time or any other rush season. I also know that many farmers who have increased their acreage over the years must now either dispose of some of their holdings or discontinue farming altogether. Last year, when we had a fairly good season and the crops were satisfactory, many farmers had to leave bales in the field because they could not get farm labourers to draw them in. I myself approached the unemployment insurance office in Saskatoon, but although there were many labourers on the unemployed list, casual labourers, they did not want to take the work because they said "If we go out we will not be able to put

Supply-Labour
stamps into our unemployment insurance books." They said had farm labourers been covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act they would be glad to come out and have an opportunity to put these stamps on their books, thus extending their eligibility for unemployment insurance.
Over the years since 1958 this matter has been raised in the house more than once, and from all sides of the house. There seem to be many members who are in full agreement that the farm labourer should be dealt with in the same way as other labourers, and it is time this was done. The commission report, dealing with administrative difficulties, says there is difficulty on account of a father and son claiming unemployment insurance, but that problem does not apply only to farm families. This is a difficulty which concerns other employees too, and I suggest regulations could be introduced to prevent such collusion.
I know the minister is very anxious to have his estimates approved and I shall not take much more of his time, except to ask him to take into consideration my representations and the representations of many farm organizations and other interested parties, in seeing that the farm labourer is brought under the Unemployment Insurance Act, the same as other segments of our labour force. In my opinion the time is long overdue for this discriminatory section in the act to be removed.

Mr. Chairman, I have read with considerable interest the remarks of the Minister of Labour when introducing his estimates. I do not intend, and I do not believe anybody in this party intends, to prolong introductory remarks because there are so many fields the minister touched upon that will require detailed questioning as we deal with the estimates item by item.
The most serious problem is that of unemployment, which has been dealt with by the hon. member for Kootenay East on behalf of this party, and by other party spokesmen. On January 30 the Minister of Labour dealt with this topic more or less at the tail end of his speech and did not express too much concern about the unemployment figures, other than to reiterate that on the basis of those figures things were looking up.
The latest figures issued by the dominion bureau of statistics indicate that there are over 400,000 people unemployed. This is disturbing enough, but the statistics also refer to 374,000 people claimants for unemployment insurance. When one relates that figure of 374,000 to the total of 414,000 it leads me immediately to question, as many have done, the accuracy of these statistics so far as the

dominion bureau is concerned. Net for one moment do I think the figure of 414,000 unemployed, serious and grave as it is, is a true reflection of the number of unemployed in the country. Winter works programs and the like take many people off the unemployment rolls for a week or ten days, and I do not think those people properly reflect the number of casual workers. I know that in years gone by discussions have taken place in parliament in which it was advocated that a committee be set up to study the accuracy of these figures.
The government has always refused to set it up.

I certainly would welcome such a committee and I may say so far as this party are concerned we challenge the accuracy of the figures. I for one accept them as a minimal indication of the number of unemployed, but I think the number is much greater. I think the sooner we have the means of getting accurate information about unemployment in this country the better it will be, especially with regard to the taking of concrete steps to deal with this problem.
As a new member of parliament I find it frustrating and disappointing to have been appointed to the industrial relations committee, which is a standing committee of this house, only to find it has never held a meeting and that presumably there is no likelihood of any meetings being held before the dissolution of this parliament. We hear screams about obstruction by this side of the house, but it should be realized that we have been sitting since September 27 and that four months have now passed during which the government could have convened this committee, when we might have examined in detail within that committee not only the accuracy of the figures and the means taken to record those figures, but the nature of the solution which has been proposed for this cancer in the economy.
The programs to which the minister has referred have been beneficial to an extent, and the idea behind them is good. However, their execution has left something to be desired, especially in urban areas. I think many of the retraining programs designed to deal with unemployment leave a great deal undone, especially in specific urban areas such as Hamilton and Toronto. Thousands of people who do not speak English adequately have come to this country in the last four or five years. They have found it almost impossible to qualify for any of these courses because of this language handicap. Yet these are the very people who are suffering most from the effects of unemployment because they are,

for the most part, construction workers; they were unskilled when they came here, and they qualified as labourers in the construction industry. They are subject to all the griefs associated with this type of work, the seasonal nature of the occupation and so on.
I would be interested to hear from the minister what concrete policies his government is willing to adopt to tackle this problem. I should like to find out whether the government, in co-operation with the provinces, has made any detailed plans for the setting up of teaching staff so this difficulty can be overcome, perhaps by arranging for a preliminary language course in connection with these training programs so that those concerned might qualify. As I indicated, there are thousands of these people involved, and they are receiving no attention from the government. A number of organizations, Italian, Ukrainian and the like, have submitted briefs to both the provincial and federal governments asking that action be taken in this regard, but they have received no concrete assurances regarding a solution of this difficulty.
I do not wish to be redundant in speaking about the seriousness of unemployment. We all know how tragic unemployment is and what a cancer it is in our society. Hon. members from urban areas understand this especially well because they are constantly exposed to the representations of those who are not able to find steady work and who do not have sufficient income to take care of their families. The situation is almost unbelievable when one contrasts it with the usual terms in which one thinks of Canada as being a country of wealth, prosperity and unlimited resources. We look around at each other and see how well we live and how well we dress. I think we are isolated here from what goes on in the rest of the country.
If this situation continues it can only lead to loss of confidence among these people not only in Canada but in themselves. This problem of unemployment is one which all the resources of government should be centralized to cure. It is the foremost and outstanding problem now before the present administration. In my opinion it is questionable whether the Department of Labour has the facilities needed to cope with it. So it has come up with stopgap measures. The winter works program is, I believe, strictly a stopgap measure. I do not see in it the promise which the Minister of Labour discerns, one reason being that it requires such large scale financial participation by the municipality in order to make it work. The government, as hon. members know, contributes only labour costs. How long can the municipalities go on submitting these
Supply-Labour
projects in the light of their depleted treasuries and constantly growing financial responsibility?
I know this question arises as far as Hamilton is concerned, because with regard to unemployment Hamilton at times attains the status of a depressed area. It is my belief we shall not be able to submit many more applications under this winter works program simply because the civic budget will not stand the strain. Thus we shall not be able to take advantage of even the temporary benefits which accrue under this program.
I have pointed out the shortcomings of the training programs as far as they affect new Canadians. It would be highly interesting, I think, to have a breakdown of the unemployment figures showing the racial origins of those without work, the length of time they have been in this country and so on. I think those figures would be a surprising revelation. Obviously the Department of Labour has been unable to find any solution to unemployment except stop gap measures. I do not think that is the fault of the department itself. I think because of its very nature the department is limited in what it can do. It will require all the resources of the government as well as of the department directly concerned in order to tackle this question; it will need monetary and economic policies designed expressly for its solution.
The speech from the throne indicated that the government intended to present a bold new program to combat unemployment. Well, several new boards have been or are to be set up. There is the national economic development board, the Atlantic development board and the manpower adjustment council which is going to set up yet another board. But it should be remembered that after four months we still have not got the national economic development board. On the other hand, having looked at the terms of the bill, which seem to me devoid of any substance, it appears questionable how effective this board would be, especially in the absence of any statement from the government about its relation with the other boards, some of which I have mentioned. I suggest the government has dragged its feet with regard to explaining the power this board would have to set economic goals.
The minister referred to the national productivity council and talked about consultation which had taken place between management and labour, but nowhere in his speech could I find any indication of precisely how the government intends to implement the findings of the mission to Europe or the

Supply-Labour
discussions which took place at the conference. They obviously came to the conclusion that certain government action was required in this area, but nowhere do we see any concrete, detailed government planning into which any of the opposition parties can put their teeth so as to implement their findings. Obviously the only way we can implement the findings, not only of the mission to Europe but resulting from consultations across the country, is by some type of legislation which we have not yet seen.
It has often been expressed by many speakers in this house, and I reiterate, that it would appear the government does not really and sincerely advocate planning in order to combat our problems. Without going into the origin of this idea I think we all agree now that something has to be done and that planning should be instituted. Until we pass the concrete measures which are necessary in order to show in what direction this country is going and how we intend to combat this problem, this tragic condition of unemployment will continue.
Another matter sadly lacking in the opening speech of the minister is any indication of the basic philosophy which lies behind his department's program. We do not have any indication of how we stand in relation to labour. Perhaps this lacuna has gone on year after year and it is felt that it is not necessary. As a new member looking at the estimates of the department, there seem to be certain basic principles and tenets which the department accepts and adheres to as far as the rights of labour and management are concerned, and perhaps the department is prepared to acknowledge this. Or maybe it feels that this is too controversial and will not even indicate a general philosophy in these two areas.
I think before the department can realistically go into all these matters of conciliation procedures, the encouragement of labour-management co-operation, and economic and research areas, they certainly must have a basic program of beliefs as far as the rights of labour are concerned. I see no government position-and I think this is an area where you would expect it-enunciated with respect to employees of the civil service and their demand for collective bargaining rights and arbitration. That is not even referred to. To my mind a general statement outlining the estimates and activities of the department for the forthcoming year would be just the place. Again perhaps this is an area of responsibility which the Department of Labour wishes to evade.
Nowhere do I see any basic philosophies or beliefs on the part of the Department of
[Mr. Munro.l
Labour with respect to minimum wage legislation, weekly working hours or vacations with pay. I think every country has accepted certain standard regulations with respect to these questions, but not Canada. Apparently it is an area which the Department of Labour wants to avoid. I think when we go over the estimates item by item it will be seen that the government must be prepared to take their stand on these controversial matters.
In conclusion all I can say, coming from an urban area with a great amount of unemployment, is that I am terribly disappointed to find there has really been no concrete action taken by the government other than, as I say, a winter works program and what I consider to be stopgap, temporary measures. There has been no concrete long range program or policy enunciated by the Minister of Labour to show in what direction his department is going, or in what direction the government intends to go in the forthcoming years to cure a cancer such as 6.3 per cent of our labour force out of work. Until the government and the Minister of Labour are prepared to come before this house and the Canadian people and show, apart from temporary measures, a longe range program of how they intend to cope with this question and provide for one million more jobs in the next five years, there will be no satisfaction in the government indicated either by this opposition or by the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks I should like to put on the record at this time. In keeping with the spirit of cooperation which our party is exhibiting in passing these estimates, I will use up only a portion of the time which would normally be available to me.
I should like to say something about the unemployment problem. I have read with a great deal of interest the speech of the minister delivered at the commencement of our consideration of his estimates, particularly the section dealing with unemployment. The most disturbing thing about the minister's speech with regard to the question of unemployment was that it exhibited a smug, selfsatisfied attitude toward this problem. It indicates that as far as the government is concerned unemployment is treated as an inconvenient problem which it does not know how to deal with and somehow wishes would quietly fade away.
I think the real trouble, or one of the troubles, is that since this parliament assembled and began discussing problems such as unemployment both the government and the official opposition have treated the whole problem as some sort of statistical matter. We have spent hours in this house listening to

the government and the official opposition arguing between themselves as to who had the highest rate of unemployment when they were respectively misgoverning the country. We have heard these endless quarrels, and the result of all this shadow boxing, treating unemployment as just a mass of statistics, is that we are losing track of the fact that people who are out of work are not statistics. They are men and women with children. They are Canadians.
Every week end my office in my constituency, which is an urban one, is flooded with people who are out of work and who are bringing problems they ask us to try to solve. The most discouraging thing about this is that with the policies in effect in Canada today, with the lack of programming which seems to face us, there is no way in which I can hold out any real hope to these people that jobs will become available for them. The minister tells us that there is only 6.3 per cent of the work force out of work, instead of 6.4 per cent at the same time last year. This is very nice and we are very glad to hear it, but the fact remains that there are still 414,000 people in this country unemployed. This means in reality that the cold, ruthless hand of unemployment is reaching out and gripping the lives of nearly a million Canadians, if you add to the number of unemployed their families and the other people depending upon them.
Where is our sense of urgency about this problem? Why must we always consider it merely a statistical matter? Where is our belief and our determination that the problem of unemployment is not a statistical question but is one of the most pressing, vital and compelling problems facing Canada today? Why can we not get rid of this passive acceptance of unemployment, this smug idea that all these people out of work is somehow a normal thing and that there is nothing very much we can do about it; that it happens every winter, and we are just going to have to endure the fact that a million of our fellow Canadians are being affected by it?
Let us try to look at this problem in terms of what it is like to be unemployed. For example, the maximum income obtainable under unemployment insurance is $33 a week.
It is $36.

Well, $36; it does not really matter that much. I have with me the brochure of the Montreal council of social agencies in which they have examined the problems of family life in Canada and set out the minimum requirements for adequate living. If we take a family of a man, his wife and two children we find that just for 27507-3-212
Supply-Labour
the bare subsistence level they are obliged to spend $87 a month on food, $14 a month on fuel and $70 a month on rent. This is a total of $171, a figure which exceeds the maximum amount which they can obtain in a month under unemployment insurance.
What does this mean to the man who is unemployed? It means that even if he is able to adequately feed his family and keep his premises, he will have no money left over with which to pay the mortgage on his home, taxes, light, or water, anything for clothing, or to have anything at all left over for recreation. This is what it is like to be on unemployment insurance.
These are the statistics we are talking about. These are the conditions under which our fellow Canadians are forced to live in this society of ours today. No bills can be paid. Mortgages fall behind. Insurance policies lapse. Creditors chase them. There are garnishee orders and court actions. Tension grows in the family. A sense of frustration develops in the man of the house, and it is not long before he begins to feel that our society does not really care about him, that he is an inconvenient problem and ought to go away somewhere. How are we going to justify our system to this man? Why should he continue to have faith in a society which does not really care about him and which is prepared to cast him aside?
It is because week after week we see conditions of this kind in our ridings that we are nauseated by the monthly spectacle of the Minister of Labour. Every month when the unemployment statistics are released we have this nauseating spectacle of the minister doing a dance of joy because there are only 414,000 persons out of work instead of 550,000. It is a dreadful spectacle for us to witness.
If one looks at the people whose unemployment insurance benefits have run out and who are forced to take welfare, one finds that the situation is even worse. A single person is allowed $7.45 a week for food and $5.75 a week for furnished, heated shelter. Nobody could even exist on an allowance of that type. A man with a wife and family is allowed $42.95 a month for heated accommodation and $64.50 a month for food. Again, Mr. Chairman, these are the conditions under which we are suggesting that our fellow Canadians should live.
I say that behind the statistics lies a tale of national tragedy and national suffering which ought to make us in this chamber ashamed of the unemployment situation. That is why when I commenced my remarks I asked this question. Where is our sense of

Supply-Labour
urgency about this matter? Why can we not recognize that the unemployment problem is probably one of the greatest questions confronting our country? Why can we not set full employment as an objective of government? As I said previously, I do not think we in this House of Commons really understand what our fellow Canadians are going through. Sometimes I think that we here are five or six light years removed from reality.
I should like to suggest that the entire cabinet and the whole House of Commons have their parliamentary salaries suspended and that they be placed on unemployment insurance for three months. I should like to suggest that the hon. gentlemen in the other place have their salaries suspended and that they go on welfare for three months. Let the members of the House of Commons and the members of the other place try to live on the income on which one million Canadians are being obliged to live. I suggest that, when the three months were over, we would come back here very much convinced of the urgency of this matter and very much prepared to do something about it, and to bring in a program that we have failed to bring in up to this time.

Why did not
your party help us in this house during the last four years in our opposition to the government because it did nothing? We had to fight all alone.
They did as much as your government did.

Here we go again, Mr. Chairman, with the old shadow boxing back and forth. Every time this matter is raised the hon. member for Essex East has some inane comment to make about the government, and they have the same comments to make about him. It is the old shadow boxing back and forth between the two old parties. They do not have an answer for this problem. They do not have any programs that are designed to cure it. Because they do not wish to face up to it they spend all their time in this House of Commons fighting each other back and forth, trying to justify the situation.
What about your party?

That is all we get from the old parties. The Liberal party is no better than the Conservative party. It has not a program either, in spite of all the hogwash they are trying to deliver in this House of Commons.
Just a family quarrel.
Loud but limited cheers.

As I was saying, the future problems of unemployment will become even more difficult. The members of our party and the members of the other opposition parties have tried to emphasize the fact that the whole problem of unemployment will become even greater in the years ahead; that the number of children between the ages of 14 and 19 who are still at school, probably 1,200,000 or more, whose education is acting as a dam to hold them back, one of these days will begin to spill on the labour market at the rate of a quarter of a million a year. We have the increasing dislocation through automation mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I think the minister should be very much worried about the statistics.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that we have had a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product. That is a very good thing. It is one of the best years we have ever had. However, in the same year unemployment dropped by only 1 per cent, something which gives the ominous information that automation is working far faster than any of us thought it might work, and that even a large growth such as that which we had last year is not sufficient significantly to cut into the very large core of existing unemployment.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose for lunch I had been setting forth the view that unemployment as it now exists will probably continue to be an even greater problem in the future. This will be due to the increased displacement of workers as a result of the inroads of automation, because of the very large number of young people who will be coming on the labour market at the rate of a quarter of a million a year, because of immigration and because of the need to eat into the very large backlog of unemployment which we now have in Canada. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it is not unfair to say that if some sort of action is not taken now to prepare for these difficulties in the future we will be building for ourselves a problem of almost nightmare proportions.
Those of us in the house who come from urban ridings have sat here since the session started last September and have listened with patience to all the problems of the farm people in Canada and the problems of other sections of the country. We have been glad to hear their problems and to see them getting

solved but I feel it is about time that we got down to the problems of the city people too. While we have sat patiently up until this time we will not sit patiently too much longer.
I was pointing out before the recess the great human hardship and suffering that unemployment brings to families, but more than that it constitutes a great waste to the community. It is interesting that Mr. Willard Wirtz, secretary of labour in the United States, said in testifying before one of their committees:
I find it almost intolerable that the country takes unemployment with such a degree of acquiescence.
He went on to say:
I am appalled by the realization that we lost more man hours in unemployment last year than we lost from strikes in 35 years.
This indicates to some degree the great loss to the community, the great loss to the country in production and income as a result of the high levels of unemployment we have endured. One thing is certain, I think, and that is that we will never deal with unemployment in Canada on the basis of an insurance scheme, nor will we ever really deal with it on the basis of a welfare scheme. In both regards we are still chasing a will-o'-the-wisp.
The solution to unemployment lies in far deeper problems in our country, problems of growth, problems of expansion. It is only when these are taken care of that we have any real chance of solving unemployment at all. That is why I was urging this morning that the house and the government accept the idea of full employment as a national goal in itself instead of chasing the will-o'-the-wisp of a balanced budget. What we should really do is that all our energies, skills and resources should be devoted to and concentrated on the great national goal of eradicating unemployment. For those of us from urban ridings who go back to our constituencies on the week ends and see the results of unemployment, it is a sickening and frustrating thing that leaves everybody whose lives it touches with a feeling of helplessness and with a feeling that the rest of the country has forgotten about it.
Today in the house we have heard very little that would encourage us to think that the government is really serious about this matter. I know the Minister of Labour is a man of good will and undoubtedly he is doing his best, but like everybody else in the house he must be frustrated by the indecision and the lack of leadership we have received from this government. I hope that when we hear from him again we will not be treated to another Alice in Wonderland tour of Canada and that he will tell us what plans the government has in mind to meet this problem. To date we have heard very little in this regard.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The fact is that many people in Canada are unable to find jobs. If any members of the government do not know this, I will be glad to prove it to them. Sometimes, as the hon. member for Danforth said a few minutes ago, people forget what it means for unemployed people to be unable to find jobs and to be on relief month after month. I, like the hon. member for Danforth and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, see these people continuously whenever I am in Toronto. Believe me, the people who come to my office and who write to me from Davenport about their desperate need to find jobs do not find it too encouraging when people across the aisle make the sort of remarks they have just been making. This is a serious subject and should be dealt with in a serious manner. There is a very personal subject, and it

represents human tragedy for thousands of people in this country who, in the last six years, have been unable to find jobs. There are two problems in particular that must be tackled if we are to restore prosperity in Canada and cure the unemployment problem. I have not got the time this afternoon to deal with all the problems, but I am going to mention two. The first of these is the annual deficits we have been incurring in our transactions with other countries. I would like to say a few words about this because I think it is central to our whole economic problem.
In 1961 the deficit in our transactions with other countries was just under $1 billion, and while the figures for 1962 are not yet available it has been predicted by ministers of the crown that the deficit will again be just about a billion dollars. The deficit in 1961 was made up of an imbalance in our transactions with the United States of roughly $1,400 million, with a surplus in our transactions with all other countries of the world combined of about $400 million. This imbalance in our transactions with the United States, means that we have been importing some of the things that we could have been producing ourselves in Canada, or alternatively that we have been unable to find markets for some of the goods we could produce for export.
They were one of our best customers.

Is that the Prime Minister speaking? It was estimated a year or so ago, by a well known economist in western Canada, that if we could bring our international accounts into balance it would be the equivalent of producing roughly 200,000 more jobs in Canada. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, if we are sincere, and we certainly should be, about getting to the root and doing something about this unemployment problem, instead of wasting time in the way we have in the last five years, we should have been dealing with the balance of payments problem. There is no simple way of doing it. It has got to be done on an industry by industry basis.

The problem became acute in 1956; it has remained acute from 1956 until now, and nothing has been done about it.

If we are going to do anything about this problem, if we are going to cure unemployment in Canada, we must approach it on an industry by industry basis. There is no simple way, by waving a wand or making a speech, to cure the problem. It requires action and that is what we badly need in Canada.
The other day reference was made to the automobile industry and on other occasions I have used this as an example of what should be done in order to solve this problem of our balance of payments. In 1961, and again that is the year for which the latest figures are available, we imported approximately $360 million worth of automobile parts into Canada. We believe that a separate department of industry should be created to deal with this problem, and that one of its functions should be to go to the automobile industry and say that the government has concluded that this very large amount of imports should be reduced by, say, two thirds over a period of a year or so-two years at the very most. That in itself would produce an extra 35,000 to 45,000 jobs in Canada in places like Windsor and Oshawa.

To go back to my example of the automobile industry I suggest that the appropriate arm of the government-and in my view it should be a separate department of industry-having decided upon the target should then call in representatives of the industry and ask, "How do you recommend we should accomplish this objective quickly and without adding to costs?" I suggest that representatives of the industry be consulted, because after all they are the people who are most familiar with the technical processes and who can provide valuable assistance to the government in this sort of thing if they are consulted. I also suggest that labour unions be consulted in a matter of this kind. In our view, in doing this if the industries concerned can suggest ways by which they can increase exports instead of reducing imports that will be so much the better.
The royal commission of which Professor Bladen was chairman suggested a formula which in principle has a lot to recommend it. It is this formula, or a modification of it, which was introduced last October by the Minister of Finance. I thought that move was a good one. It was a move in the right direction, but it did not really go far enough. That particular move if it is successful, as the minister stated at the time, might reduce the imbalance in our transactions so far as automobile parts are concerned to the extent of $30 odd million. That is an insignificantly small part of a $360 million deficit in that particular industry. It did not in my view show any real sense of urgency in tackling this problem.
There are many other industries which will have to be dealt with in exactly the same way. During the past four months various members on this side of the house have been meeting privately and have worked out plans which could be made applicable to many other industries in Canada. This approach would go

a long way toward reducing this tremendous imbalance in our international transactions. We would be well on the road to reducing unemployment in Canada to levels at least considerably lower than those we have today. That is the kind of approach which is needed. We are not going to solve this problem by shouting at each other across the House of Commons. We can only solve it if we start oft with some real understanding of the difficulty and then, with determination and a power of decision, do something about it.
The second of the two problems which I said must be tackled head on if we really intend to balance our international transactions, restore prosperity and cure unemployment in this country is of a different kind. It has nothing directly to do with the balance of payments question. It is the unsatisfactory and much too low rate of investment in Canada in both the private and public sectors of the economy. As far as investment in the private sector is concerned, there is a great need to expand existing industry and to develop new industries in Canada. I am one of those who would prefer to see this done by private investment because I believe in the decentralization of decision making, particularly when we see how difficult it is for some governments to make decisions of any kind. However, I think we must recognize that there is in private hands in Canada a shortage of the kind of capital which is needed in order to expand certain industries. Certainly there is a shortage of the kind of capital needed to develop new undertakings in the extractive industries. In the past we have allowed too many of these developments to be financed by foreign capital and that is, in my view, one of the reasons why we are facing the problems which confront us today.
While on balance I should prefer to see as much private capital as possible invested in such undertakings, if it were available, I certainly would not like to see the expansion of industry and the development of new projects curtailed merely because there is a shortage of private capital for such purposes. In that event it seems to me that public capital should be made available. What was done in the case of the Polymer Corporation is an excellent example.
Remember the shoe factory in Saskatchewan.

I am not thinking about small shoe factories and other things which were done in Saskatchewan. The hon. member can ask his friends over there in the New Democratic party to talk about Saskatchewan at the proper time. I am saying that if it is a question of unemployment or of investing public funds in new developments then we should use public funds for such purposes.

Now, in what is usually looked upon as the public sector of our economy it seems to me that if we in Canada are to resolve our unemployment problem, restore the prosperity of our nation, and make our cities and towns better places in which to live and work we should make grants and low interest loans available to municipalities. This would permit them to get on with the job of improving our cities and towns and, in the process, stimulate the construction industry in Canada and thus provide the kind of jobs which can only be provided in that industry. The Liberal party has proposed that this should be done through a municipal loans fund and I suggest that the sooner a loan fund of this kind is created and the earlier we get on with projects of this sort the better it will be for the people in my riding of Davenport, the people in Danforth, the people in Winnipeg North Centre and the people in a lot of other ridings in this country who need that type of work. In some cases it is the only kind of work they are accustomed to doing. I, for one, would prefer to see public moneys spent in that way than that they should be spent in keeping these people unhappily on relief which, as a previous speaker has pointed out, means misery not only for the head of the family but frustration and difficulty for all its members. Sooner or later this represents a big bill in terms of broken homes and-I do not like the phrase "juvenile delinquency", but it is the one which comes to mind.
I cannot this afternoon, certainly not on the estimates of the Department of Labour, outline a complete program of what the Liberal party would do to deal with unemployment in this country.
It would be agreeable to me if the hon. member for Davenport would do that.

All right, I will come back later and do it. At this stage I wished to outline two major aspects of our program for dealing with unemployment. One is to bring our international accounts into some kind of balance by producing ourselves some of the things we are importing, as well as by exporting more of the things we can produce. The second item in this program is the creation of a municipal development fund which would really put some juice into the construction industry and provide many more jobs.
