Yes.
Supply-Labour

Thank you very much. I am glad to have this opportunity of continuing because I was talking about this problem of our balance of payments in western Canada a few weeks ago and I pointed out then that this imbalance in our international transactions had a great deal to do with bringing on the financial and exchange crisis last year. I suggested that if we fail to put our national house in order, if we fail to clean up the mess we see around us, we run the risk of facing another financial crisis.
I tried to find out this morning from the Minister of Finance whether he had any ideas about when he might ask for further interim supply in order to carry on the business of the country for the present month of February because this government has run out of money and will soon be unable to pay its bills. If this is the way the government runs its own affairs or runs the affairs of the country, it does not leave me, and I doubt whether it leaves many other people, with very much confidence as to what we may expect to encounter in the near future. It is clear evidence that the government does not know how to manage its own affairs. And surely that means it is incapable of dealing effectively with the question of finding work for Canadians.
By a strange coincidence, shortly after I made the remarks to which I referred, the sometimes invisible Minister without Portfolio made a speech in Toronto to the Toronto board of trade. It was last Monday, January 28, and I should like to read two sentences from one paragraph of this speech. He said:
Those who go around this country predicting crises in its foreign exchange position, predicting economic calamity internally, should give serious consideration to their position as Canadians. This is still a free country-
-said Senator McCutcheon-
-and if I felt as they appear to feel I would pack up and leave.
That is the end of the quotation. Senator McCutcheon analysed the economic picture for the benefit of the large audience he was addressing, and then made that comment. I suggest that this is an incredible statement for a member of any government to make. It is an incredible statement even from a non-elected member of an arrogant government like the present one. There are four to five hundred thousand Canadians without jobs at the present time and the ones I have talked to are critical of the government, very critical. Does the hon. senator suggest that they should all move out? If so, may I ask him where he thinks they should go and who is going to pay their bills?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is a disappointing interpretation.

Supply-Labour
You are.

Hon. members on this side of the house

Mr. Chairman, there seem to be murmurings going on, but I am not going to pay any attention to them.
They cannot swallow their own words.

If they have anything to say they can get up and I will be glad to hear them in due course. Hon. members on this side of the house, myself included, have been highly critical of the government's incapacity and indecision, of its inability to come to grips with any problem, of the frightful failure it has made in dealing with this human, personal problem of unemployment, with all the misery which that word implies. So I say to the Minister without Portfolio and to the members of his government that we intend to stay in Canada. We have a responsibility to stay under our democratic parliamentary system, and if after an election-which I was about to say can be only weeks away, but perhaps is only hours or days away; I noticed the Prime Minister did not answer the question whether he saw the Governor General yesterday-if after the election we are called upon, we intend to clean up the mess that this government has got our country into. And we intend to do something to cure the unemployment problem.

Mr. Chairman, I might say that the reason I gave my consent for the hon. member to have additional time was that he intimated that he would put forward a program on behalf of the Liberal party which he would put into effect should that party become the government, and I am sorry indeed that he took advantage of that time without saying a word about it.

Mr. Chairman, since this house went into labour yesterday the pains seem to be coming more frequently and severely. I should like to say that we in this party are not happy with the levels of unemployment which we see in Canada today. Furthermore, whether or not they are less than or equal with the levels of last year, or even the preceding year, is not a valid argument for saying that the levels are all right. I think the Minister of Labour agrees that he is not satisfied with these levels, but I must say in all fairness that some of the charges being made to the effect that nothing is being done simply are not true. I know that there are not particularly large numbers of unemployed in my constituency, but there is far more unemployment than I like to see. I also know that, as has been stated time after time both in this house and outside, even though
IMr. Nesbitt.]
it may not be as bad as it was at some other time, if you are unemployed it is bad at any time.
There is one other matter we are going to have to give a great deal of consideration to, namely some of the recommendations made in the Gill committee report. This is, in my opinion, a very agonizing reappraisal of the unemployment insurance commission, and if we were to implement these recommendations suddenly there would be some adjustments which would be very painful. I think there are some good recommendations in this report, and perhaps most of them can be implemented gradually. I want to say a little more later on about some of the things being done to try to solve the unemployment problem, but I am not going to let some of the remarks of the hon. member who preceded me pass without a comment or two.
For example, he mentioned the shortage of private capital in Canada as being one of the major contributing factors in the unemployment problem, that is to say, that because of this there are not sufficient jobs being created. He also mentioned-at least, I took this meaning from what he said-that this was also the reason which aggravated the problem of investment of foreign capital in the industry of Canada. I agree that this is certainly true.
I think the reason that private industry has difficulty in finding the long term capital requirements needed for expansion is that the federal government is in the private money market on such a level, forcing the interest rates up to such a level that private industry is a little bit hesitant about taking on long term commitments at these interest rates, which are established in competition with the federal government. I suggest that it is in line with Social Credit policy that public capital for social expansion should be provided by the Bank of Canada, and that the government should move out of the private money market and leave private capital for private enterprise.
There are two or three other points I should like to make. I am not going to speak for very long. One is the matter of the increasing unemployment problem in the flour milling industry. I raise this matter specifically because that is one section in the labour market in which we have steady increases from one year to the next. If you go back and compare this year with last year, last year with the previous year and so on, you find that in each succeeding year more plant capacity is being shut down in this particular industry. What I should like to suggest is that the Minister of Labour use his influence with

the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce so that in some of these wheat deals we have been making some portion of the total volume could be delivered in the form of flour.
A few months ago I had the privilege of visiting in Africa. In one of the countries there I found a brand new, almost automatic flour milling plant which, in fact, turns out something like 8,000 hundredweight of flour per day. This figure is 2,000 hundredweight per day more than the total domestic requirements of that country. Here we see a situation in which they are importing all of the wheat they need to make flour. They are providing a few jobs, but they are also providing some national income; so I do not blame them for setting it up. However, the fact is that we are supplying them with the raw materials and they are processing them, when we have right here in Canada the plants and the men who could be doing this same job.
I should like to read into the record a little bit of information to show what has happened to the flour milling industry, as of just a few weeks ago. For example, there is one mill in Medicine Hat that is completely closed down. Another one is running at about 50 per cent of capacity. Another one is running at about 55 per cent of capacity. I understand there is a plant at Goderich, Ontario, that is completely shut down and another one at Peterborough that is shut down. There is one at Brantford that is shut down. There is a plant at Port Colborne, with a capacity of 26,000 hundredweight daily which is now operating at a rate of 7,000 hundredweight daily. At Keewatin there is one plant which is completely shut down, and there is another mill which is running only part time. In Winnipeg there is a mill that is being remodelled. It is shut down completely now and is in the process of renovation. It bad a capacity of 7,000 hundredweight daily. After the remodelling is completed, its capacity is going to be reduced to 3,000 hundredweight daily. All the mills in Calgary are running much below capacity. There is at least one that is completely shut down there, if not two. The largest mill in Lethbridge, Alberta, is running at below 50 per cent of capacity. This situation is fairly serious. I believe that some relief should be given to this situation if the Canadian negotiators, in our export marketing of wheat, would try to have some flour included in the total deal. I understand that in one of the wheat deals made with red China, for example, one of the provisions was that they should take some of the wheat in the form of flour, but that this has not been done.
Supply-Labour
We know that there is competition in this field, and I fully appreciate that fact. I believe that the United States government are providing some wheat subsidies that are applied to flour being exported. We also know that there are perhaps some lower labour charges that go into the production of flour in some of these other countries. At the same time, however, since we grow the raw materials here I think we should be concentrating on trying to provide some of the finished products as well.
If I may, I should like to deal just for a moment with some of the things that I think are being done. I am not saying that they are adequate or that they are completely doing the job. However, a few things are being done about solving this unemployment problem. One of the major things that has happened recently is the action that was taken by this government in co-operation with the provincial government in providing vocational training schools and schemes. It was only last week that the keys to the one built in Medicine Hat were turned over to the local school board. I should like to congratulate all of those responsible not only in that constituency but all over Canada for the good work they have done in setting up this kind of plant. We realize that they were breaking new ground nearly all the way. It is a tremendous undertaking to line up courses, curricula, staff and all of the other things required when there is not anything to look at-more or less set up a program to follow, if I may put the matter in that way. For example, for the one in Medicine Hat-and I am not sure that this applies to other schools as well-we had to find journeymen and people who were skilled in many trades and technicians who did not have any teacher training. So they have hired a number of people who had the skills they were supposed to teach, and now they have them on the staff and they are taking teacher training so that they will have the ability to pass that information on.
In Medicine Hat there have been outlined programs which have been prepared with a view to better meeting the ability, interests and needs of six groups of students. They include, first of all, the business education group. Then there is the vocational group, the technical group, the professional matriculation group, the pre-employment group and the adult group. It should be pointed out that these new programs are the inevitable outcome of, for example-at least this is the premise which is used in working out these programs-of the rapid advances in technology which are changing the entire pattern of industrial occupations and the demand for more workers with higher levels of technical knowledge and skills. Then the other problem

Supply-Labour
they looked at was the school drop-out problem which sees large numbers of young people entering the world of work unprepared to meet its demands. Then there is the need for a new program more adequately designed better to meet the ever widening range of pupil abilities and interests.
In the business education branch, for example, they are working out programs for secretarial training, including shorthand, typing, office practice and so on. They are working out bookkeeping and clerical training, and retail clerical training. Then there is a special one year course for graduate students and those with 70 high school credits will concentrate training in skills for office work. I think this program is very important but there are other programs and other parts to the programs. There are industrial, vocational and beauty culture programs, and in this particular area I do not believe there is any precedent anywhere in Canada as to what might be included in the programs to turn out students with the required skills. As I mentioned, there is a technical and vocational program and with regard to this particular segment I think this short paragraph is rather significant. They say that prospects for employment for this technically trained group are excellent, and go on to say:
Up until about 1959 a large percentage of our technicians came to us from Europe and the British Isles. This is no longer the case and Canada must educate its own technicians.
Obviously we have the people in the ranks of the unemployed and if they take this training Canada will not only be provided with people to do the work in this field but we will also not have to bring in people to do these jobs, though I have no objection to immigration at all. They are also setting up three and four year matriculation programs for those who would like to enter a profession, as well as pre-employment programs and adult education programs that will be carried on at different hours when the school is not being used by the regular students.
There is only one other point I want to make and that will conclude my contribution to this debate for the present. While I was overseas visiting some of what have been commonly referred to as the emerging nations of Africa I was struck immediately by the almost complete lack of a middle class in their social and economic structure. In Nigeria, for example, they have opened five new universities in the last two and a half or three years or since the program started. This will certainly provide highly trained persons in specialized fields and perhaps in general as well, but there is a problem in that large numbers of workers are required to provide the supporting administrative staffs

for these university graduates. They do not have any facilities for training this type of student.
It must also be recognized that the entrance requirements for vocational training schools would be substantially lower than for universities and such schools widen the possibilities for people without university qualifications to get some kind of training that will fit them for a useful life. I believe that those of us who have looked at the new vocational training schools recently built in Canada are aware that there is space available for a greater number of students. I am not too familiar with the situation in other parts of Canada but I know that in Alberta so much capacity has been provided that some of it will be unused in the immediate future.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Labour that through the Department of External Affairs the government invite some of these countries to send students to Canada to make use of the extra capacity we have now, because I really believe that there is a very great need for technically trained people in those countries. Certainly it would be a great contribution toward helping them to help themselves. We cannot provide all of the technically trained people they need to operate their industries, but we can invite them to send some young people here who will undertake to learn a trade and acquire teaching skills so that they can go back to their countries and in turn train more people.
In my opinion this is by far the best kind of foreign aid that Canada can provide, the kind of assistance that will help these people to help themselves. They do not want us or anyone else over there running their affairs for them, but they recognize that we have made advances in education and technical skills from which they can profit. It is our responsibility to help them and I hope that something can be done to invite these governments to make use of the facilities we now have. As I said, I do not think we are going to be able to use all of our capacity immediately.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very carefully to the speech made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) last January 30, when he introduced his department's estimates. His remarks were impatiently awaited because the unemployment situation remains serious in our country.
The minister spoke about the activities of his department in the fields of research, economics, conciliation, civilian retraining, etc.
All these subjects are no doubt interesting but, as the representative of a riding made

up mostly of working people, like many of my colleagues, in the name of the unemployed who have been forsaken in the last few years by the Conservative government, I must complain once again about the complete lack of interest shown by the minister, once more, in the speech he made last Wednesday about the most important problem in Canada today, that of unemployment.
In fact, when the minister states that the unemployment problem is serious, we would expect him to show us, through his estimates, that short-term concrete steps are being taken to deal with that situation immediately.
Well, apart from the winter works program to which I shall refer later on, the minister has done nothing except leave the unemployed to their own fate and, unless favourable circumstances come up unexpectedly, circumstances with which the Conservative party will have had nothing to do, we shall have to face the fact that those unemployed will receive, this year, nothing but their unemployment insurance benefits and unemployment assistance payments.
To my way of thinking, Mr. Chairman, it is time the government should realize that the unemployed cannot pay his rent, his doctor and even less his grocer with statistics.
I said earlier that the unemployed was left to his fate because this year the government brings in no new short term measure to solve that problem and it is quite easy to prove it.
In fact, the 1962-63 estimates exceed by only $47 million those of 1961-62. Now, I challenge the Minister of Labour to prove that a substantial portion of those $47 million will be used to implement short term projects which will be of some assistance to the unemployed in this country before the year is out.
Mr. Chairman, we cannot expect a substantial increase in the winter works program this year, and the minister knows it. If you refer to page 3268 of Hansard, you will see that the federal contribution to those projects will amount to $35 million while they amounted to $34 million for the fiscal year 1960-61.
Again I ask the question: apart from the winter works program, what short term measures is the government considering to help the unemployed? The answer is none. There were none to be found in the speech from the throne, none in the minister's statement. We shall again have this year the same situation in this respect that we had last year and the years before.
Supply-Labour
We know that the minister, in all his statements, stresses the fact that there has been a continuous increase in the number of people in Canada who are working. As if there was anything new in that, when in a country such as ours there is a constant natural increase in population. I submit that this is a very poor screen to use to hide not only an unfortunate situation that has been going on for too long, but also the government's inaction and lack of imagination and boldness concerning the unemployment problem.
What is, in fact, the extent of unemployment right now, in February 1963? What do the statistics show? That, possibly, is the most important aspect of the question, but the minister carefully avoided it in the speech he made on January 30, as shown on page 3272 of the official report, where he said:
In December unemployment reached a total of 6.3 per cent of the labour force, compared to 6.4 per cent a year earlier and 8.2 per cent in 1960.
How can you discuss intelligently a problem such as unemployment if you do not know its scope and its ramifications? At the end of January 1963, I asked the following question: How many unemployed are drawing unemployment insurance benefits in Canada?
How is it that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), who answers in the house for the unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service, cannot tell us, in introducing his estimates, how many unemployed are drawing unemployment insurance benefits in Canada right now? Why conceal that information which I consider as essential to all these discussions on unemployment?
But I should like to discuss that matter a little further. A few days ago, on January 28, I put question No. 1,324 on the order paper and asked the minister for the following information:
What are the latest statistics of the unemployment insurance commission concerning the number of unemployed persons who are receiving unemployment insurance benefits?
The minister answered that at the end of November 1962, the number was 347,000.
Now, I ask the minister this question: How can he explain that concerning such an important matter, the only statistics available to answer my question of January 28 were those available at the end of November 1962?
Is it that our employment service or the unemployment insurance organization is so

inadequate that it is impossible for a member of parliament to know the number of unemployed receiving benefits for a period of less than two months? I do not believe that.
I know that the minister has the most recent figures in hand. I know that every week he gets figures from the various offices.
It is, I think, very strange and most unfortunate that members of parliament are unable to secure the information they believe necessary, at least in a discussion like the one we are having now.

This is an extraordinary attitude on the part of the minister.
You made the charge.

He is asking a member to prove that the minister is receiving weekly reports from his officers. Here is another important problem that the minister avoided mentioning and I take this opportunity-

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that the minister was sleeping during the last few minutes I was speaking. I have already said I asked this question and that I received an answer. I had even mentioned that the amount is now $98 million. That is not the point. I say to the minister that he

Mr. Chairman, I was saying that there are now only $98 million in the unemployment insurance fund, and I would like to stop here for a moment to recall a particular fact to the Conservative and Social Credit members who are conspicuous by their absence.
When the Liberal administration is blamed for unemployment, I ask them to remember a very important fact: when the new administration took over in 1957, there were $926 million in the unemployment insurance fund. Now, if one considers that we had then $926 million in the fund, that answers the childish argument often raised by the hon. member for Villeneuve. So, Mr. Chairman, we must make the best of it.

Even though I have never considered them as anything more than an unemployment index, the figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics show most eloquently that we have a serious situation on our hands.
Mr. Chairman, a few years ago, the present Minister of Labour claimed that there was a state of national emergency when, in 1954 and 1956, the unemployment level reached only half of what it is today. He seems to have forgotten the speeches he made in those days.
Mr. Chairman, we must realize that the government is at present going through a most serious crisis. I know that if I was unemployed I would consider myself in a desperate situation. There is nothing to expect from the government which has remained at the helm because it had the support of the Social Credit party about which I will have a few things to say in a moment.
I hope that in the near future the voters of this country will be given an opportunity

of electing a stable administration, a majority government and none but the party I belong to will ever be able to lead this country toward prosperity because it will prove that if in the past it has succeeded in creating full employment in a country such as Canada, it can repeat the performance.
Mr. Chairman, I admit that the government pays 50 per cent of the labour costs involved in the winter works program, but I wish to point out to the minister that the government of the province of Quebec is the only one to supplement this program with a 40 per cent contribution program of its own.
And what did it do?

Has the question been put? I would like to say a few words on unemployment in the province of Quebec, Mr. Chairman. Its causes can readily be traced. For several years, the provincial authorities refused to accept from Ottawa the money which Quebec taxpayers contributed to the federal government's coffers, and which they were entitled to get back in part. I think that in the provinces which, today, are suffering much more than others, we might have extended this works program over the whole year and also doubled the government's share.
If the winter works program costs the government $35 million, I think nobody can pretend that we cannot double our contribution in the present circumstances when provinces like Quebec, for instance, and others, are facing the most acute unemployment problem.
Mr. Chairman, I would now like to say a word about our hon. friends of the Social Credit party. I want to tell them that they are quite as responsible as the Conservative members for the present situation. They systematically supported this government, when they were quite aware that the throne speech mentioned nothing but the winter works program to solve the unemployment problem.
The unemployed in Canada will not forget that if the government has been able to

hang on to power these last few months, if it has been able to survive in spite of its inaction these past few years, it is thanks to our Social Credit friends who have placed the interests of their party above those of their country.
This is the last opportunity I will have to remind the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) that the first duty of a member of parliament is to attend the sittings of the house, not to look after the organization of his party.
Mr. Chairman, the Social Credit members who have participated in this debate on unemployment would have us believe that the solution is to be found in their monetary theory. I do not have the time to challenge that contention now, but I should like to ask the hon. member for Villeneuve-

According to the Social Credit members who spoke during this debate, the adoption of their monetary theory would be one way of creating full employment in Canada. If the hon. member for Villeneuve does participate in this discussion, I would ask him to comment on the following. During the last election campaign, when he stated before Canadian workers that the monetary theory of Social Credit would be one way of fighting unemployment, why did both his leader and himself hide from their audience that in 1956, their monetary theory was condemned as inflationary by a royal commission in New Zealand and that since then, Social Credit has never been heard from in that country? I ask the hon. member for Villeneuve why he tries to deceive the people by telling them that his theory could solve the problem.
Mr. Chairman, in concluding may I say this: My hon. friends of the Social Credit should not worry, they will soon pay for having supported a government which they knew very well was unable to settle any situation at all; but they did it precisely in a petty party interest.
I am convinced this is the last time we shall have the opportunity of studying the estimates of the Department of Labour. The situation is hopeless. The unemployed have completely lost confidence and hope in the

government. They will soon be asked to judge it again and they will take advantage of the occasion to judge also the hon. members of the Social Credit who, to this date, did but one thing in the House of Commons, namely fill the shoes of the Conservative members they had defeated.
Would the hon. member allow a question? Does he agree with Mr. Le-sage that unemployment is a provincial responsibility, as he said during the 1960 election campaign?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He never said that.

The hon. member is giving me the opportunity of paying tribute to the premier of Quebec, for the courage he has shown in this regard. In fact, he was the first among all provincial premiers, to recognize that unemployment was a national problem, that could not be solved without the co-operation of the federal, provincial, and municipal governments.

I have asked a question to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and the hon. member for Laurier has replied that Mr. Lesage had never said that, while the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont replied that it was a provincial responsibility. I should like to know who of the two is right?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if you will allow me, I will say that the question was badly put, because the hon. member has asked whether Mr. Lesage said it was a provincial responsibility. Mr. Lesage never said that; he said it was a responsibility which must be shared between the three levels of government, as my colleague has just said.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Earlier today my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard pointed out that yesterday and today we have been discussing two of the most important questions which are facing us, on the one hand the question of what we are going to do about nuclear weapons and on the other hand the question of unemployment, the subject which has occupied most of our time today.
I find it interesting that this parliament* for all its faults, has been discussing these two important questions yesterday and today. I find it particularly interesting in view of the rumours and reports which are drifting: into this chamber.

About half an hour ago a report came in that the Prime Minister was at government house. I suppose he was just taking tea with the Governor General or recommending some appointment, but he could have been doing something else. The most recent report is that he is back in the east block.
Order.
What is the hon. member talking about?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am talking about the labour estimates.
Oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am beginning to wonder, in view of the reports that are coming in, whether this parliament is going to have a chance to complete the labour estimates or any other estimates. As a matter of fact, the prediction I made on December 17 may well come true. Maybe we shall go through the fiscal year 1962-63 without parliament approving the estimates.

I wonder if the hon. gentleman will permit a question. Does he know of a rumour, widely current, that the Prime Minister has already slipped through the tunnel to the West Block en route to an unknown destination?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Apparently the hon. member has had an even later report than I have had.
He has a pipe line.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I am reminded, of course, that this is February 1, 1963, and that on February 1, 1958, just five years ago today, the Prime Minister went to see the governor general of that day and at six o'clock made an interesting announcement to the house.
If these rumours and reports foretell what we are going to be doing in the next couple of months, I am glad that we have had before parliament in these two days these two important issues, one concerning nuclear weapons and the other the question of unemployment. I urge most strongly on all members of this house in all parties that they should throw away some of their prejudice about words and do some really hard thinking about ways and means of providing full employment.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech made a little while ago by the hon. member for Davenport. I felt, as I sat here, that I was watching an idea struggling to be born in the mind of the hon. member. He expressed great concern about unemployment and about the numbers of Canadians without jobs, and insisted that it was not good enough for us to shout across the chamber at each other about it, but that we
Supply-Labour
must do something about unemployment. In particular, he called upon the government to do something about unemployment. He said by way of defending his own party in the matter that some of the members of his party had discussed this question and had made plans to deal with some of the problems which affect our economy. A little later, after he bowed three times in the direction of private enterprise, he got bold enough to-say that it might even be necessary to invest large sums of public capital in our economy to provide jobs for our people.
As I say, I enjoyed watching an idea struggling to come to birth in the mind of the hon. member for Davenport, but as he made his speech he carefully avoided facing up to the fact that if we are to do something about full employment we have to go in for democratic economic planning. Members of other parties, though they know that something of this sort has to be done, still regard these words as something to shy away from, because of their loyalty to the kind of system we now have. From the speeches which have been made today on all sides about the importance and urgency of the unemployment problem, a problem which may be talked about a good deal in the next couple of months if today's reports have anything to-them, it must be realized that if this problem is the serious one it is in our country it is not good enough to go on arguing about statistics and the amount of money in the unemployment insurance fund. Surely the time has come for that sort of over-all economic planning which will get our economy rolling and provide a situation in which, as one of my colleagues said this morning, there are more jobs than there are people to fill them. Only when we reach that stage will we be in the position of having full employment in this country.
In addition to this problem there are many other items of unfinished business as far as the Minister of Labour and his department are concerned. There is the question of doing something about labour legislation in the field of minimum wages, statutory holidays, and holidays with pay. Then there is the question of improving the vacations with pay act. Improvements need to be made so far as government legislation is concerned in the provisions for collective bargaining. The time has come for the government to pay heed to principles it supported at the international labour conference with regard to consultation among government, employers and labour in the matter of employment. All these are things which affect our people. The time has come to do something about the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is strange that with the Gill committee report in front of us, the-Minister of Labour found it possible to make

Supply-Labour
his opening remarks the other day without indicating when the government planned to act on that report by way ol legislation.
I promised myself, Mr. Chairman, even if I did not promise the committee, that I would make my remarks brief at this point, and I intend to do so. But I do urge that this whole problem of unemployment be looked at not just as something to talk about or as an area in which we argue over figures, but as a problem which calls for the best thinking and brains which we have in this country, and for sound over-all economic planning.
I am glad to see that the Prime Minister is back in the chamber. This at least puts a stop to any more rumours that he is at point A, B or C. He is now here and can tell us later, if he wishes, whether he has seen the Governor General, whether he has been through the tunnel, and so on. If that is so and if the event of February 1, 1958, is to be repeated on February 1, 1963, the people of Canada will get the chance to hear from all parties in this country where they stand on the important issue we discussed yesterday and on the important issue of full employment which we are discussing now on these labour estimates.

speechtext:
I am advised by the Clerk that there is a member of the Liberal party who will rise after you, so I suggest you take the floor now.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to take part in the debate on the estimates of the Department of Labour. But
after hearing the rather humorous and strange remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets), a Liberal member as one might expect-who stated that Social Crediters in this house were more concerned about the party's interest than the country's-I feel I should say a few words. The hon. member should know something about the policy of putting the party's interest before that of the country for a great number of years, in fact for over 22 years, he followed it himself within the Liberal party, when he sat in the Canadian parliament.
He added that the hon. member for Villeneuve was seldom in the house and that he was doing organization work for his party.
It is obvious that we want to get rid of incompetents like him in this house. This is very definite and quite in order. Besides, I said it publicly and I repeat it in this chamber: Elections are not won in the house, they are won outside. But I still come to the house often enough to take part in the debates and I have spoken more often than the hon. member himself since he has been sitting here.
Moreover, when he says that we deceive the voters by supporting or voting with the Conservatives when want of confidence motions are presented, I point out to the hon. member that we do not deceive the voters, that we think first of the interest of the country, and that is why we do not play the Liberals' game when they try to set traps for us, here and there, in order to catch off guard the members of the other opposition parties or even some government members.
Mr. Chairman, those considerations will enlighten the public on the attitude we have taken in the house. That does not mean that we support the government as such.
A moment ago, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon. member will agree that the Chair has allowed him a lot of latitude up to this moment. I think perhaps he should now get back to item one of the labour estimates.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, those are remarks which you have allowed the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont to make a moment ago. If the hon. member has the right to attack the member for Villeneuve, I wonder why you would prevent the latter from replying adequately to the former.

(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I should advise the hon. member tor Villeneuve that the Chair is being very tolerant. I realize that during the last part of the speech of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont I allowed him some leeway, but I hope the hon. member for Villeneuve will come back to vote No. 1 of the labour estimates as quickly as possible.
(Translation):

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I come back at once to the subject matter of the debate, the estimates of the Department of Labour. We get more and more complaints from everywhere. I receive complaints from my constituents, of course, but many of them come from all over the province and all over the country. They are directed against the Department of Labour which does not seem to understand its responsibilities with regard to Canadian workers.
For instance, this sad story appeared on page 3 of the Ottawa Citizen of yesterday:
(Text):
An unemployed father of five school-age children, who says he cannot find work, was sentenced to 40 days In county jail this morning for defrauding the unemployment insurance commission.
George David, 55, of 45 Skead rd., was sentenced to five days in jail on each of eight charges to run consecutively. He pleaded guilty to receiving an overpayment of $181 from the commission.
"I can't look on this as anything but eight cases of outright theft," said Magistrate L. A. Sherwood.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to discuss the legality of the sentence imposed on a 55 year old man, a father of five, who was charged with over-collecting an amount of $181, while he claims that he has already paid back $39. But when a man who is unemployed and collects $181 from the unemployment insurance commission is prosecuted and sentenced to 40 days imprisonment, I say to myself that the unemployment insurance commission, which comes under the direct jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour, should change its attitude or its rules so that our Canadian fathers are not treated that way right here in the Ottawa-Hull region, or indeed in any region.
And the article goes on:
(Text):
He said that up until last year he had worked all his life and never drawn unemployment insurance.
David claimed he didn't understand papers he signed which stated he did not have employment while he was collecting the insurance.
"They said to me 'you're good for collecting for one year'," he told the magistrate. "I thought it was money coming to me. I am on relief and unemployed."
Supply-Labour
He is on relief and unemployed, with five children and his wife at home. The article continues:
The accused said he had gone to two Ottawa controllers for work "and they turned me away."
"When I went to the unemployment insurance office they told me I was too old," he said.
That is at 55 years of age, Mr. Chairman. I would ask you to take note of that. We all know that at 55 years of age you are too old right across Canada today. This is why we think the Minister of Labour should look a little more closely at the social legislation in our country. The article continues:
"My lights were shut off and my children were hungry."
David said his children range in age from five to 12 years.
Hugh Johnstone, an investigator for the UIC, said David had made the statements "and he knew what he was doing".
At one point David and Johnstone were shouting at one another across the courtroom, David claiming he had repaid $39 and Johnstone claiming he had not.
John Murchison, lawyer for the accused, asked the UIC investigator if leniency "or a blind eye" was not sometimes shown by the UIC in some
cases.
"I've never known that to happen," was the reply.
David said when he went to the UIC "I gave the lady my book, she stamped it, and that was all there was to it".
However, that man with a family is in jail. He is in jail for 40 days accused of having committed what they call a theft of $181. We have seen many cases like that one, not only here in Ottawa but across the whole country.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be amended.
We are at present discussing the estimates of the Department of Labour. These amounts have already been spent. In Canada, from coast to coast, winter works are in progress.
Some minutes ago, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont told us that we should extend and expand the winter works program. Personally, I feel that all that program can do is help out momentarily a very small portion of the Canadian population; it cannot solve the hard core of our unemployment problem.
I am convinced that there are other ways. By all means, let us pass the estimates, and pay back those provinces which have taken part in the winter works program. But it is imperative to modify the labour legislation if we want to avoid in the future cases like the one about which I was telling the house.

Supply-Labour
I believe there is enough room in Canada outside jailhouses to allow individuals to select their own kind of work, instead of condemning them to prison under the pretence that they have obtained sums that were not due to them at the time.
Mr. Chairman, Social Crediters have neither a pro-government nor an anti-government attitude. They take solid stands to secure the enactment of a labour legislation which would enable Canadians to find work, live in comfort with adequate means in a country capable of offering each and everyone of its people freedom over and above security.
(Text):

We have heard a great deal about unemployment during this session. On innumerable occasions we have been told that this is our No. 1 problem; that it is a terrible thing; that it bears in on the lives of hundreds of thousands of Canadians; that it destroys their personal freedom and their will to live. We have also heard that we should do some hard thinking about this problem. We have heard a great many words in general terms about solutions. Certainly we have had the blame placed by speakers for each party on all the other parties in the house.
I should like to speak briefly this afternoon about a few tangible things that can be done about unemployment in areas in which a great number of people are out of work. We do not want government in all phases of industrial activity but government certainly must participate and is going to have to participate effectively when there is substantial unemployment, and in places where many people are out of work.
There are vast projects which are possible, the timing of which can be advanced by government investment at an early stage, per-ihaps in research, certainly in construction. One of the largest projects which could appeal to Canadians in the immediate future is the construction of a crude oil pipe line from the west in northern Alberta to the Montreal area. In the west of Canada we have in the Athabasca tar sands an oil reserve which is as large as the proven oil reserves of the conventional type in all the rest of the world, and processes are currently under development which promise to result in the production of that oil at a reasonable price.
There is the problem of disposing of the oil in Alberta. There is too much oil now and if the oil from the tar sands were suddenly to bear in on markets now available to the conventional oil producers it could create chaos. Why not gear a large pipe line development to that oil resource? Support, if

necessary, research in the processing of that oil from the tar sands and make the oil available to Montreal in a market which constitutes nearly 40 per cent of the Canadian requirement. This market is largely supplied at present from Venezuela and the Middle East. This would mean not only the saving of hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign exchange and help our balance of payments but would also mean several thousands of continuing jobs in northern Alberta. A vast complex would evolve there financed, principally, I believe, by private capital and of the order of the development in Sarnia, Ontario, today. During the construction phase the vast steel companies at Hamilton and Sault Ste. Marie in the east would be busy producing steel, cement companies would be producing cement and other companies would be producing other construction materials and certainly machinery and equipment would be in great demand.
This type of development can be promoted by public investment if private capital is not immediately willing to carry out the entire project. Certainly it will be supplemented by private investment. This is the type of thing which a government concerned about unemployment would investigate seriously now and have under way in the next few years if we continue to have 5, 6 or 7 per cent of our labour force out of work.
There are other projects. Our uranium mining industry was geared to a sudden requirement of large proportions in the United States. That requirement has largely ceased. United States mines are supplying that which remains. Our uranium mining industry has been laying off people and will continue to lay off people. What can be done? I believe government can do something about this. We do not have within the borders of this country a processing facility for converting uranium into the enriched high grade forms which are necessary for many types of power reactors. Europe will be the first to require nuclear power on a large scale. Certainly we will want to sell to Europe and today we cannot. We cannot sell because we have to sell to the processing plants in the United States owned by the American government. The priority, therefore, obviously is to the American mines.
So I believe that government finances may be necessary in order to build a processing facility such as I have in mind. This would be of the order of an Arvida or a Kitimat. In a period of five to ten years it would provide jobs for 5,000 to 10,000 people. This is the type of thing which government may have to get into, perhaps totally in the early

stages because of the element of secrecy involved, but this would provide a real hope for our uranium mining industry. This is the type of tangible project that we should be talking about rather than generalities or general policies with little meaning.
There are other projects. Research and development should be aimed, I believe, at the processing of the ash from some of our western Canadian coals. In these ashes lies an aluminium source of the type that the Germans used to make aluminium during the last war. We do not produce any of the aluminium source materials in this country. We bring in all our bauxite and alumina from the Caribbean and from Africa. Our mines branch could, by investigating processes of this type, make possible a large aluminium industry based firmly on the coal resources of western Canada. Tremendous resources of this type exist and I believe that there we could have substantially self-sufficient industries which did not involve foreign exchange and which did not involve our purchasing materials outside our country and providing employment outside our country, but rather jobs right here in this country. We have these great possibilities.
The Columbia river treaty could result in a series of projects of the dimensions of the entire Ontario hydro installations today. Literally thousands of people would be employed within the next few months, certainly within the next few years, in the construction of these projects and this great international development. I believe that with good will on all sides, not only across the border but between parties in this house and between governments in this country vast projects of that type could get under way and more work could be provided in areas of serious unemployment.
Governments have to get together. Certainly the province of British Columbia has not been working very well with the government in Ottawa and, I suggest, vice versa. I believe it is possible for instance, on the river with which I am familiar, the Fraser river, to have great multipurpose developments not only for power projects but for flood control, irrigation and so on. The northwestern corner of the United States has been favoured because Washington has looked on that part of the United States as an area in which to stimulate this type of multipurpose development by providing low interest loans and by providing engineering, economic and research services free through the United States army corps of engineers. We could do this through some other governmental device in this country.
Supply-Labour
We could get other major projects going. The North and South Saskatchewan rivers are interprovincial in character. Multipurpose developments are possible there. Certainly developments of a similar character are possible in other provinces, including the mari-times where unemployment is a serious problem. I believe these projects could provide tens of thousands of jobs, but of even greater importance in terms of greater employment are our service industries. Tourism is one of these. In the Vancouver area we have a remarkable situation. Few people who did not live there would believe that most Canadians there go to the United States to ski. They go south of the border for their winter sports. Yet within a few miles of Vancouver we have some of the finest scenery in the world. Federal and provincial cooperation in respect of highways and in the development of park areas could provide not only great immediate employment opportunities but the springboard for great service industries, a great tourist industry, a great convention centre industry in that part of the world. The west coast has a great deal to offer and it can offer many more jobs sooner if vision of that type is shown.
We have heard a great deal recently about the national economic development board. Perhaps it will supersede the national productivity council, but under its terms of reference projects are mentioned. I have mentioned a number of projects of the type which can be carried forward. I hope that the Department of Labour, through an effective minister of labour and an effective staff, will be able to spot these projects, assist other departments to find projects and work as well with industry and labour in order to bring forward the types of sdhemes which can provide many jobs.
Government initiative is needed. Certainly government planning is needed. I believe we should rely wherever possible on private enterprise and private initiative, but in the private enterprise economy there has been at least periodically serious unemployment and we must deal head on with this problem.
I believe the keynote really is co-operation between government and industry, government and labour, between governments in this country and, in view of the incidents of the last few days, between governments across international boundaries. I think that with the will to co-operate we can beat this unemployment problem and I hope this afternoon I have given a few tangible ideas as to how we can get at it soon.

Mr. Chairman, I want to speak in connection with an act that is administered by the Department of Labour, the Industrial

Supply-Labour
Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. This is a rather fantastic situation in which I am involved personally, and in order to put the situation into focus I have to put on the record a letter from 2167 Barnes street, Montreal, dated October 20, 1962. It is addressed to Mr. John M. Paquet, national president of the Canadian trainmen's union, 344-15th street, Limoilou, Quebec. This letter is signed by J. Earl White, national organizer of the Canadian trainmen's union. It reads: Dear Mr. Paquet:
Re: Interview with Messrs. Robert Beaule and Mr. Real Caouette.
After our meeting in Quebec city on October 17 I took your letter of introduction to Mr. Beaule and arrived in his office the following morning.
I was promptly received and discussed the C.T.U. platform with Mr. Beaule. He was quite familiar with it and is prepared to support the cause for which we also fight.
Mr. Beaule asked me to wait in his office and he searched around the building until he found Mr. Caouette. They returned to Mr. Beaule's office.
The interview with Mr. Caouette was very brief. I asked him first if he was familiar with section 6 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. He was quite familiar with it and very much opposed to the compulsory feature of it because the compulsory feature took away from Canadian labouring men the rights supposedly given to them in the Canadian Bill of Rights.
I told Mr. Caouette that I believed that 80 per cent of Canadian labouring men were opposed to compulsory membership and compulsory dues, because it weakens rather than strengthens labour unions in their dealings with management.
I suggested that his party should advertise their support of a change in the industrial relations act to eliminate compulsion. Mr. Caouette stated it was already the policy of his party and that they were doing a great deal about it.
I suggested that his party should arrange to interview 100 labour union members by picking them at random on the street in various Canadian cities. I told him that I was convinced that he could draw large numbers of votes away from all the political parties and in particular the New Democratic party-if he made it clear that he favoured democratic Canadian labour unions.
I then asked him to introduce in the House of Commons an amendment to the industrial relations act at this session of parliament, because Prime Minister Diefenbaker must respect the wishes of the Social Credit party if he wishes to remain in power.
Mr. Caouette thanked me very profusely for the suggestion and he stated that he would recommend it to a caucus of his party and that he was quite sure that positive action would be taken on the suggestion in the near future.
Just as we shook hands and Mr. Caouette was about to depart a man appeared at the office door looking for Mr. Caouette. Mr. Caouette invited him to come over to where we were and then invited us all to be seated. This man was a stranger to me and I was not introduced to him. Mr. Caouette then asked me to repeat what I had just suggested to him. I did so and finished up by saying that as far as the labouring vote was concerned his party could massacre the other three parties and especially the N.D.P. Mr. Caouette thanked me again and left the office with the stranger whom he still did not introduce.

After they were gone Mr. Beaule asked me if I knew who the man was and I admitted that I did not. Mr. Beaule then told me that the stranger was Mr. Douglas Fisher, M.P. for Port Arthur and a top rank leader in the C.C.F. party.
Mr. Beaule assured me that Mr. Caouette is a very smart politician and that he is sure that he has a very good reason for letting Mr. Fisher know immediately on what basis he proposes to put pressure on Prime Minister Diefenbaker.
I cannot imagine what Mr. Caouette's strategy is other than to cause the New Democratic party to vote to support Diefenbaker in a vote of confidence over the question of compulsion in our so-called democratic American labour union. Such a development could prove to be very embarrassing to the N.D.P. and the C.L.C.
I am arranging to send a supply of C.T.U. letters and miscellaneous material to Mr. Beaule. I was very pleased to observe that he already had a file of considerable proportions-thanks to your initiative.
The developments presently occurring in the House of Commons are encouraging in the extreme.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, this letter is signed by J. Earl White, national organizer of the Canadian trainmen's union. There are a couple of things that need to be put into focus here. This letter came to me from a union organizer or representative in the Quebec city area. He informed me that it has been distributed fairly widely amongst railway employees in that part of Quebec, particularly on the Canadian National Railways. It has been distributed with the argument that here, in effect, is a New Democratic party member visiting Mr. Caouette and apparently approving of Mr. Caouette's views that section 6 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act should be altered so that there is no check-off of dues allowed to any unions which come under federal jurisdiction.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this is a fantastic conclusion to draw from what I am sure the hon. member for Villeneuve will remember and acknowledge was an innocuous visit on my part to his office in order to chat with him about some ideas he wanted to express to me if I was going to write an article in a newspaper about him. I think the hon. member will acknowledge that. To find, as a result of that very brief visit to interview Mr. Caouette about some information for a newspaper that I am identified with the Social Credit party's view on breaking an important part of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is just going too far.
I am not attempting, Mr. Chairman, to make accusations where the hon. member for Villeneuve is concerned or his colleague referred to in the letter, Mr. Robert Beaule, but it is quite apparent that this Canadian trainmen's union is capable of jumping to some fantastic conclusions. I should like to point out, therefore, that this is a union that does not have a contract with any major

railway in Canada. It is what we call an attempt to destroy a union that is already in existence and serving the men. I should like to refer to the proceedings of the committee which examined the Canadian National Railways, but since the Anal report has not been received, I cannot give evidence from that.
However, I believe I can say that the hon. member for Lapointe at that committee revealed he was in favour of this Canadian trainmen's union and completely ignorant of the relationship of the brotherhood of railway trainmen to the railways of this country and the responsibilities that they carry out. I would like to point out that section 6 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which permits a check-off, was challenged in the courts, and it is my understanding it was upheld as being good law by Chief Justice McRuer, and since that particular incident it has stood.
If the members of the Social Credit party wish to make this part of their campaign, and suggest they want this taken out and that they do not want the check-off for labour union men in Canada, then that is fine; but it is not only fantastic, it is dastardly, that as a result of a chance visit to the office of the hon. member for Villeneuve I am identified as being in favour of this. This is coincidence run wild.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that my reception in the few minutes I was in the office of the hon. member for Villeneuve was adequate and friendly, as one expects in all relationships with members of other political parties; but I must say that this gentleman, in describing the incident, has not been completely factual, because the hon. member for Villeneuve did not ask him to repeat the gist of his argument so that I could hear it at all. That did not take place.
This particular personal issue, and I emphasize it is a personal one, has very serious implications in a general way. Recently in Canada, particularly with the upsurge of the Social Credit party in Quebec, we have had a fantastic kind of approach to labour unions. These gentlemen seem to feel that the rights that have been hard won by labour unions- and many labour unions feel they should secure many more-have gone far too far and must be cut back. One of the means of doing this is to weaken and cripple the unions.
At this particular time the railways are going through a state of flux and change. There has been a steady reduction in the number of jobs available. It is an unstable situation and there is a tremendous need for co-operation and liaison, not only between management and labour but much more
Supply-Labour
so between labour unions. In this connection I would like to argue it would be vital to consider seriously the kind of suggestion that apparently-if we believe this letter- the Social Credit party wants to put forward, which in effect would go a long way to destroy these unions that represent the working men on the railways.
So far as the Canadian trainmen's union is concerned its emphasis is remarkably upon a kind of Canadian nationalism that is extremely narrow. If any members of the house feel it is time for the so-called international unions to end their relationships with international officers in the United States, that is an opinion or point of view to which they are welcome, and they are welcome to argue it; but this is no reason to go in the face of the tremendous contribution that Canadian unionism receives from the United States, a contribution that in many ways still exists and is still coming in so many fields.
I feel, particularly in the railway business where we have the illustration of an all Canadian union, the Canadian brotherhood of railway and general employees, working very strongly with the international brotherhoods on the non-op side, that we have proof we can have a Canadian union on the railways that will do its job and work with brotherhoods that have international relationships, and that both can work together for the workmen on the railways and the trade union movement as a whole.
This being the situation I would ask the Minister of Labour to dismiss in a very cavalier fashion the kind of arguments put forward by organizations such as the Canadian trainmen's union that would somehow suggest, because a member of parliament happens to come into the office of another, that he is all set on ruining one of the most important pieces of legislation that is on the statute books today.

Mr. Chairman, there are three definitions I wish to put before the committee in talking in this labour estimates debate, and I hope they will assist in clarifying the objectives which I am sure all of us have for those Canadians whose livelihood and happiness are dependant on the employment policies of the government. These definitions are as follows:
1.	Unemployment is the involuntary idleness of a worker seeking work at prevailing wages.
2.	Job, a regular remunerative employment.
3.	Employment is the degree or extent to which persons needing employment and who are available for employment are provided

Supply-Labour
with employment, or lack of it, because of the prevailing economic conditions. Employment in a particular area, and this is very important in the definition, is likely to increase or decrease according to the economic conditions of the country as a whole.
This may seem very academic, but I feel that unless we constantly attempt to find out what is wrong with the economic conditions in the country that allow us to have a chronic rate of unemployment, then the Minister of Labour will not be able to effect a cure for the country.
I suggest that the minister's greatest concern will be the employment policies and practices of his government, and not just the unemployment problem. I am sure he agrees with this proposition. Yesterday the minister stated that unemployment is still a very grave problem. That is right, and it is an extremely personal one for hundreds of thousands of our people. However, Mr. Chairman, I think the government has an even greater problem on its hands, and until it has answered that problem we can really look for no significant change in the job picture for our people.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
I must explain that this measure does not deal with such an angelic nuisance as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. It has to do with material nuisance in relation to our national resources.
I am introducing this bill once again because I am alarmed at the sight of our industries and people polluting our waters, as it were, with their own hands at an increasing rate. Over many parts of Canada the water table is falling, yet thousands of factories and hundreds of municipal sewer systems are discharging their waste into our rivers with only a fraction of this increasing filth having been given adequate previous treatment. We all know that water is the life blood of any country, yet though we have more than trebled our consumption in recent years we are polluting it and destroying the watersheds whence it comes. We are destroying something without which we cannot survive and for which there is no substitute.

There are substitutes for power and for other materials but there is no substitute for clear water.
The soul of man, shaken and bruised by the ceaseless din of modern cities and the calamitous international sabre rattling, needs treeways rather than freeways; it needs pure waterways rather than sewer ways. We are disfiguring the natural landscape, eroding our soil, destroying our forests and polluting our waters almost with the zeal of a religious mission in the name of so-called progress. The purpose of this bill is to make it an offence for the owners of industrial plants and oil refineries or other persons to discharge noxious matter into an interprovincial water, thus endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public.
It provides as follows:
Every owner, lessee, or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, sawmill or other plant or works, or any other person, who discharges or throws or allows to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product, raw sewage, oil, sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river, stream or other water any part of which is interprovincial or which flows into any interprovincial water, which has the effect of endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public is guilty of-
-either an indictable offence or an offence punishable on summary conviction.
This measure is identical with one which was introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was a distinguished and militant member of the opposition. In this respect it can be said, for once, that by introducing this bill I am following in the footsteps of John. It must be agreed that the scope of the bill is limited. It deals only with the provision of pollution of interprovincial rivers. I think this question arose on that earlier occasion as a result of the Saskatchewan river on the Alberta side of the Saskatchewan boundary. There was a great deal of concern at that time on the part of members representing the province of Saskatchewan in this house. Nevertheless, this is a short step which we can take to indicate where we stand on this matter in this house- to show our concern and willingness to do something within our powers to correct a situation which is becoming increasingly bad.
I have had a lifelong interest in the question of conservation. I have lived very close to the soil, to the waters and to the woods of this country and I have had a close relationship throughout the years with persons who have held opinions similar to my own. But in presenting these views this afternoon I am introducing a bill which members of this group support wholeheartedly because they realize we cannot maintain a satisfactory material standard of living for the generations
Criminal Code
to come unless it is based on adequate national resources. We aim to preserve our heritage for future generations. As I have said before, water is of prime importance, though many people fail to realize it. I think the government of Canada failed to realize it when they signed the Columbia treaty and made it possible for the United States to use for all time the surplus waters of the Columbia for irrigation and domestic purposes as well as for flood control, rather than preserve those surplus waters for use in the Okanagan and, some day, for the irrigation of the western prairies.
Considerable interest has been taken in this matter throughout the years by small numbers of people. The international joint commission has done some excellent work with respect to agreements with local authorities, and measures for the prevention of pollution in certain international waters. There are numbers of provincial organizations in British Columbia and in the western provinces, in Ontario and the maritimes, which have taken a great interest in this question of the prevention of pollution of rivers and streams. There are other groups, not so well known, perhaps, which carry on their work without much publicity in the municipalities, besides numerous individuals in various occupations in life, particularly in some of our universities and research establishments. These people have pointed the finger at the desperate need for federal, provincial and municipal cooperation to meet this situation. I must say, in fairness, before proceeding further, that I give this government credit for a limited approach in making provision to assist municipalities to obtain sewage disposal plants. That is all to the good, but it is far too timid an approach really to accomplish the objective outlined by the minister when he introduced his legislation.
In dealing with this question I should like to quote from a monthly letter issued by the Royal Bank of Canada. In it is an article entitled "Resources for Living". I will give credit to the Royal Bank of Canada for the interesting articles they have published with respect to the conservation of natural resources. They must have someone at the head of that institution who understands this problem and is interested in it. I quote briefly from page 3:
The purity of our air and water and the foods produced on our soil and in the sea will determine our number, our health, our efficiency, and our enjoyment of life.
Although pollution has reached impressive proportions, legislation competent to eliminate it is creeping forward at a snail's pace.
This group wholeheartedly agrees with that statement.

Criminal Code
There is delay in initiating measures of cleanliness because of lack of clearly defined responsibilities. The various levels of government are not certain who should do what. As was said in a paper presented at the "Resources for Tomorrow" conference: "Indecision and delay stem in part from differences in interpretation of the B.N.A. Act and a lack of clear federal and provincial policies." Meantime, public health is at stake, recreational values are impaired, industrial uses are limited, and fisheries suffer.
That indicates the interest of prominent persons in one of our large banks in Canada and represents growing opinion in this country.
I should also like to quote briefly from the Gazette of October 5 an editorial entitled: "Why water pollution gets little action". This editorial says:
At the recent conference of the water pollution control federation in Toronto, a good point was made by Mr. K. F. Beaton of the public relations department of Shell Oil Company, New York. He said that the success or failure of efforts to control water pollution will largely depend upon the public's understanding and support of what is done, or might be attempted.
There is much to this. If water pollution control were a comparatively inexpensive thing, governments might be ready to introduce it. But it is immensely costly. It will take up many tax dollars. This expenditure may have to be taken away from some other project, or will have to delay other plans.
There is not the same general pressure for action, the same insistent demand that the huge sums of money be spent, as there might be for something like highways, where the problem seems far more visible and personal and urgent.
Yet the threat of water pollution may be one of the greatest-all the more so because it is a rising danger. But unless the public demands that something be done, or unless the public is brought to realize that something really effective must be done, the control of water pollution will likely remain where it is today-quite low on the list of priorities.
I received a very interesting magazine through the courtesy of the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Sams), who I understand is very interested in this problem. The magazine is "The Civic Administration Handbook of Environmental Pollution Control", and it deals with the subject from the point of view of municipal authorities. The handbook is about the difficulties which are related to the question of overcoming river pollution. I should like to quote from this in view of the fact that I am introducing a bill today similar to one introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). The Prime Minister sent a message to the editor of this magazine for publication, and I do wish he would give effect to his message. He said:
I congratulate the editors and publishers of civic administration on their initiative in publishing a handbook for municipal administrators on the sources, effects and control of environmental pollution, the first such publication to deal with the pollution of soil, water and air as a single problem.
[Mr. Herridge.l
Canada is fortunate to be endowed with abundant renewable resources and it is incumbent on all of us to see that in using these we do not destroy them, but pass them on unimpaired to future generations. In carrying out this trust, the control of pollution is of fundamental importance.
The letter is signed by the Prime Minister and I do hope that the members of his party will on this occasion support this bill so that it will pass this house before the hour is completed.
This matter is of increasing concern and is a danger which is growing apace. We have only to look at the Ottawa river flowing beside our parliament buildings to realize the necessity for some action. We also have this problem with many other rivers of Canada. Fortunately I come from a district where there is very little pollution, an area in which flow two great rivers, the Columbia and the Kootenay. But this problem which is facing the people because of sewage disposal from various cities and industrial developments must be nipped in the bud. We have a little problem at the present time but we must prevent it from becoming a big problem. I suggest that we need research. We need information. The public require to be informed. We need co-operation between governments. We need legislation such as this. This is first-step legislation to deal with this increasing problem. We need the participation of the Canadian people in the defence and protection of our great natural resources. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I urge support for the principle of this bill as a short step, so far as legislation is concerned, in the direction in which we should go.
