speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In my view, water pollution is fast becoming, as was expressed by the hon. member who has just spoken, one of our most pressing domestic problems as we go on developing the industrial potential of Canada. In my opinion there are two basic steps which are needed to keep pollution from reaching dangerous proportions, proportions which, as was so well described, are dangerous to our national health and wellbeing. First, efforts must be made to clean up the sources of pollution. Second, legislative action must be taken to ensure that

wastes are properly treated before being discharged into our watercourses. The views expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and his arguments in favour of this measure I think are most surely agreed to by all hon. members of this house. For regardless of the constituency from which we come, this problem has already become, or will shortly become, one of major concern to those we represent.
Mr. Speaker, the Concise Oxford Dictionary defines "water" as "a colourless, transparent, scentless compound of oxygen and hydrogen in liquid state, convertible by heat into steam and by cold into ice". I think that to go beyond the mere definition of the word it should also be stated that water is the most important of our natural resources, because there can be no existence without it and no progress where it is in short supply.
Some excellent reading for anybody interested in this topic may be found in a booklet published by the international joint commission in 1961 entitled: "Safeguarding boundary water quality". One short statement in that booklet indicating the significance of pollution reads as follows:
Pollution impairs the quality and usefulness of water. It makes it unfit for domestic or industrial use. and recreation, and may cause serious illness. It destroys fish and wildlife. It creates offensive conditions and interferes with navigation. It may create areas of desolation and render the stream useless for constructive purposes. It causes economic losses, and it reduces the capacity of the waters to perform their many beneficial and necessary functions.
I come from a constituency which is fast changing from its traditional agricultural background to one of suburban and industrial character, and while farming still plays an important part in the economy of our area, even the most rural of our municipalities have felt the pressure of growth and in several instances they have also felt the evil of water pollution.
Hamilton harbour, once the site of many fine bathing beaches and beautiful homes, has in just one generation completely degenerated into a massive pool of sewage and offensive chemicals, causing the city council to spend millions of dollars on a sewage treatment system to cope with this unfortunate problem.
Similar steps have been and are being taken by many other communities in southern Ontario. In the metropolitan Hamilton region the amount of money being spent is reaching fantastic proportions; but this must be done in order to combat the very evident hazard to health which pollution brings. These projects will, I hope, restore our waterways, especially our great lakes waterways, to their 27507-3-213
Criminal Code
former purity and beauty. However, before we legislate through the medium of the Criminal Code, as this measure would suggest, I believe we should recognize the steps taken by provincial authorities as well as the voluntary steps taken by industry in this field.
First of all, I should like to mention for a moment the steps taken by industry. A large oil refinery is located along the north shore of lake Ontario about midway between Hamilton and Toronto and, if this proposal became law, it would perhaps qualify as one of the worst possible types of offenders. As hon. members know, a concentration of phenolic waste is one of the worst contaminants in existence.
There is in Ontario legislation which would, and with some substantial effect, prohibit this plant from discharging objectionable wastes into this main interprovincial and international waterway. However, this company has undertaken to provide itself with one of the best possible examples of industrial waste treatment.
The Cities Service Oil Company has developed a $3 million conservation program, including a "green-belt" buffer zone around its plant, an air pollution prevention plan and a waste treatment plant called by its operators the most modern and most efficient anywhere in the world. According to information I have received from the company, the quantity of waste treated averages about 300 gallons a minute and, as an example of the success of the process, called biological oxidation, all traces of phenol waste are removed and the water is returned to lake Ontario in a purer state than that in which it was taken from the lake. To graphically illustrate the success of the operation-and I think this may be of particular interest to the hon. member for Kootenay West-may I say that the company has installed a large aquarium where native fish of the great lakes thrive in water which has gone through the petroleum processing plant. The treatment process incidentally enables the company to recover thousands of barrels of oil which would otherwise be lost and which would under less favourable circumstances flow out into lake Ontario to pollute that great waterway.
The example I have described is but one of a number of similar steps being undertaken in southern Ontario where industries are taking the initiative in waste treatment. I would, however, suggest that this particular company has gone far beyond its responsibilities in demonstrating to others what can be done in this important field.

Criminal Code
In Ontario, as indeed in several other provinces described by the hon. member for Kootenay West, provincial authorities have been set up to study and control pollution and related matters, and in the few minutes remaining to me I should like to outline one or two measures which have been taken in Ontario in this regard.
In 1955, recognizing the need for safeguarding Ontario water supplies and adequately dealing with the effects of pollution, especially those from which domestic water supplies were being drawn, the government of Ontario set up a committee to look into these questions, and followed it the next year with the creation of the Ontario water resources commission. In 1957, legislation was passed increasing the scope of the commission's functions. I should like to read briefly from a paragraph contained in a booklet describing its major activities. It does these things:
Supervises the operation of all water, sewage treatment and waste purification plants in Ontario, and lends technical assistance in this connection.
Keeps close watch over stream pollution through examination of streams and sources of pollution. The commission has the right of enforcement of any of its requirements to individuals, industries or municipalities in this regard ...
Advises municipalities concerning their water requirements and their needs in connection with sewage disposal and treatment. '
Reviews plans and approves or disapproves of all water and sewage projects to be undertaken by municipalities or persons . ..
Operates laboratory and research services in connection with problems relative to the fields of water, sewage and industrial wastes.
The remarkable accomplishments of this commission since its formation and the commencement of its program has led to the investment of $363 million in Ontario in an effort to combat what would be included in the Criminal Code under the bill of the hon. member.
I believe that the federal government has a place in this particular question. However, I believe that place should be a co-ordinating one between the individual provinces, each of which has a particular problem in this connection.
I agree wholeheartedly with the principle behind the proposal of the hon. member. There is in Canada today a tremendous need in federal, provincial, municipal and business circles for a complete awareness of the tragic loss to our nation of one of our finest natural resources, namely pure water. As we extend cultivation, disrobe our forests and plow our fields without regard to soil erosion and as we continually overload our waterways with the wastes of our industries and our cities, the banks of our rivers and lakes become garbage dumps for the next generation. Our

harbours have been turned into gigantic cesspools, indeed frightful products of modern civilization.
I suggest that we require much additional research, but in addition we require much additional education. We face today in Canada the complete loss of all major waterways as places of recreation. We face an impairment in the use of this water for agricultural purposes. We face an impairment in the use of this water for domestic consumption, except by expensive chemical treatment and filtration. We also face one of the most costly projects which this nation has ever undertaken, if action is not taken quickly to stop individual offenders.
Recent progress has been quite substantial in several areas in spite of serious obstacles. Perhaps the greatest stumbling block is the post-war industrial expansion and population surge in this country. We now have the opportunity of restoring a healthy state to Canadian waterways defiled for the present by a young, aggressive nation. I believe this critical situation could best be summed up by reading from the report of the joint commission on boundary waters. It states in part as follows:
The satisfactory quality of these waters in the future can be secured and maintained. They can be used and enjoyed by the people of both countries continuing as one of the greater natural resources as long as the rain falls and the rivers flow.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill No. C-27, an act to amend the Criminal Code, is to make it a criminal offence to pollute interprovincial waters, and this purpose could easily be unanimously accepted by this house. I understand, however, that as the bill is drafted it is word for word the same as a former bill drafted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was in the opposition. It seems to me that this bill is brought forward again in the same manner as it has been year after year by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) possibly in order to embarrass the Prime Minister and also so that once again it would not be supported and would be talked out. For these reasons I want to be brief so that I will not be accused of making a lengthy speech simply for the purpose of continuing until six o'clock.
I ask the hon. member for Kootenay West to amend his bill so that when an individual is found guilty of polluting interprovincial waters he will not have a $25,000 fine imposed on him, but a lesser fine. I would also ask the hon. member for Kootenay West to agree that a clause be inserted which will provide that the bill will come into force on March 31, 1963 in order that municipalities

bordering on interprovincial waters will have time to complete construction of their sewage purification plants by that date. That is the date when financial aid to the municipalities ceases, according to the amendment to the National Housing Act brought forward by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton), which extended the expiry date from March 31, 1961, to March 31, 1963. I asked for this extension before the passage of that bill.
The constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle, which I have the honour to represent, is vitally concerned. It is situated at the western end of the island of Montreal where the St. Lawrence river and the Ottawa river, both of which are considered to be interprovincial waters, join. I should like to speak on pollution problems at length and also about the water purification board recently created by the province of Quebec. I have a large file on pollution. I believe that this bill is necessary and having suggested certain changes I would ask that debate on the bill not be prolonged to six o'clock in order that passage in principle may be granted.

The hon. member for Saint John-Albert, in his usual flattering way, has said it would be impossible for me to be a nuisance, and I thank him for saying that. I feel, knowing the great admiration in which I am held by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), that, notwithstanding party differences, this is one occasion when I can sincerely follow John. It seems to me that this might be the last chance for the Prime Minister to carry out one of the promises he made to the people of Canada. I felt that I could be of assistance along with the honourable and genial member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), in assisting the Prime Minister to carry out that promise to do what he could in every way, by legislation, by administration and other ways, to end so far as possible the pollution of all these streams that come under federal jurisdiction.
I am very sincere about this, sir. For 25 years I have lived on the banks of the Ottawa river. During those 25 years the condition of the Ottawa river, the Rideau river and unfortunately also the Gatineau river, has not improved. It does seem to me that if there is one project about which it would be wonderful to do something before our national centennial, it would be to clean up these open sewers in our capital city and make these rivers once again the kind of thing of which we Canadians can be proud as part of our national heritage.

look about this distinguished chamber this afternoon, I have some suspicion that either the trains to Montreal and Toronto have broken down for some mysterious reason or else some other event is upon us. Perhaps that is so, since there has been the dry sound of clicking knitting needles from the gallery above.
I was disappointed that in an otherwise excellent debate, during which much good has been said about fellow citizens and the work they have done in this field, very little was said about one of the most impressive achievements of this government in this fight against water pollution. There has been a reference by the hon. member for Kootenay West to the municipal sewage treatment process, which I suggest to you fits clearly into this field. He described it as a very limited approach. Well, sir, I have had the advantage of obtaining from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation figures which would make the hon. member change the adjectives in that description. I think this has been an imaginative approach and one which has worked out very successfully indeed.

As of January 18 last loans under this program totalled $138 million. I should have qualified that somewhat by giving a breakdown, and if I am permitted I should like to have this table appear in Hansard for the assistance of hon. members. The breakdown is as follows, actual inquiries where municipalities are eligible for such assistance, $51,768,000; applications on hand, $2,119,000; approvals are of the order of $84,900,000, making up the total of $138,787,000.
In addition to this, there are some 72 applications now being processed for which no definite amount is known. Perhaps before proceeding I could ask if the house would be agreeable to have this table printed in Hansard. The table is headed "Loans for Municipal Sewage Treatment Projects, Summary to January 18, 1963". The breakdown is by provinces, and the total amount for Canada in the three categories I have mentioned. The figures were drawn up by those who should know, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, at my request for this debate.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. To depart for a moment from the table, I might say that municipalities from all provinces have taken advantage of this excellent program which was started, as perhaps hon. members will recall, in December, 1961. In December of last year, these provisions were extended and provided long term loans to municipalities, as well as forgiveness for certain work completed before 1963. This provision has now been extended to March 31, 1965.
I was impressed by the point made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier-Lasalle (Mr. Rock) to the effect there should be notice given to people so that the act would not suddenly fall upon them, and so they would know when the act would come into effect. This would give them an opportunity to clean up, for example, any part of an industrial
operation which polluted our water resources. I am sorry the hon. member did not put his idea in the form of a formal amendment. However, if and when the bill goes into committee, this could be done and the amendment considered. This would be really the basis upon which I should like to give my support to the bill, that is giving notice of the pollution in the first place and then stating a time within which these serious matters of water pollution could be cleared up.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West upon introducing this bill. At the outset of his speech he said he would like to see debate on it concluded by six o'clock. I know there are several other hon. members who would like to speak on it, and I am sure the hon. gentleman knows full

Criminal Code
well that I have been interested in water pollution and have spoken on bills like this previously. At one time I introduced a resolution dealing with a similar problem.
I am sure he will agree I am not in the habit of making a nuisance of myself in the house and of taking up much of the time of the house, but I want to make a few comments in regard to this bill, Bill C-27. The purpose of the bill is to make it an offence for the owners of industrial plants and oil refineries, or other persons, to discharge noxious matter into an interprovincial water, thus endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public.
I have a particular interest in the bill because lake Winnipeg lies within the boundaries of the constituency of Selkirk and we have several interprovincial rivers running into that lake. We have the North and South Saskatchewan rivers emptying into lake Winnipeg. We also have the Red river, which is an international river, and the As-siniboine river which flows into the Red river and is an interprovincial river, also emptying into the lake. Industrial waste is one of the big factors we have to contend with, and as the law stands today industry is now responsible for taking care of its industrial waste. In many cases industries find the cheapest method is to release waste into the rivers, and that is one of the main reasons why we have had our rivers polluted. However I am sure industry realizes its responsibilities and is willing to share in the cost of cleaning up the rivers.
This matter of water pollution was one of the subjects discussed at the resources for tomorrow conference held in Montreal in October, 1961. It received a lot of attention, papers were presented on the subject and workshops were set up to deal with the matter. On that occasion a paper prepared by Mr. Menzies was submitted to the conference, a paper which I have read and found to be very interesting and helpful in understanding the problem of water pollution.
Basically we are concerned with the effects of pollution. Briefly these are its effects on human life and health, fatal and contagious diseases and infections, its effect on other forms of life, fish losses through poisoning and oxygen depreciation, its effect on waterfowl and the destruction of waterfowl habitats, together with its non-fatal effects on water for domestic purposes. I may say that in Manitoba we have seen much wildlife,

many waterfowl, die from the effects of water pollution. We have seen its effects on fish and we know the danger caused by water pollution.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned that the water table was gradually falling and that pollution would become an increasingly difficult problem. I have to agree with that statement. It is becoming a greater problem; but as the hon. member for Halifax mentioned, this government took the initiative in passing legislation in 1961.
Under the provisions of that legislation loans were offered to municipalities, and as the hon. member for Halifax pointed out, the total of loans made to date is $84,900,000. When additional applications now being processed are approved, the total will be brought up to $138 million. Hon. members must remember that 25 per cent of this is nonrepayable.

In that province up to January of this year 21 loans have been made totalling $914,000, and of that 25 per cent or $225,500 will be rebated. This section of the act certainly has been effective as a start in tackling the great problem of water pollution, but I realize there is a lot yet to be done. Probably the government has to work out further plans with the provincial governments and municipalities.
The resources for tomorrow conference, when dealing with water pollution, discussed several items and I want to comment on the recommendations they made to the government at that time.
